## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{100}{20}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Why must every motion a robot follows already contain the stop it will probably never use?_

A moving robot cannot pause its momentum while a learned policy computes the next piece of its motion. Each new plan must take over from motion already under way, and a plan that matches only the arm's position leaves a jump in velocity or acceleration that the motors can meet only with a sudden step in torque, which a real drive refuses or converts into vibration, wear, and a spilled load. A path that clears every obstacle can still ask for more joint speed, torque, or current than the body can supply, and the fastest timing along that path demands exactly the abrupt changes a drive cannot make. The next plan can also arrive late, because inference time has a long tail, and a machine that keeps moving while it waits spends the distance it needs to stop. Without trajectory planning, a correct decision about where to go becomes a command the body cannot follow, or motion that cannot be halted in the room that remains. Planning attaches timing, a smooth join to the present state, and a stop that runs without the proposer, and those three properties decide whether a command that crosses the causal boundary can still be brought to rest before its energy reaches something that cannot be undone.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Distinguish prediction horizon, executed prefix, renewal cadence, and evidence age when budgeting trajectory replacement
- Map tool-space speed limits to joint rates through the manipulator Jacobian, explain why the mapping fails near a singularity, and bound an inverse-kinematics step there with damped least squares
- Evaluate a timed trajectory and its time parameterization against actuator torque, current-slew, and voltage limits, including reflected rotor inertia ($N_g^2 J_{\text{rotor}}$)
- Synthesize closed-form quintic spline bridges that eliminate acceleration steps and bound commanded jerk across replanning seams
- Size a jerk-limited $C^2$ stopping suffix from deceleration and jerk bounds and verify stopping clearance ($d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clear}}$)
- Enforce the two-tier deadline hierarchy (high-rate chunk leases versus hardware commitment cutoffs) to prevent transitions into inevitable collision states (ICS)
- Compare sampling-based search, trajectory optimization, and learned action chunking by the work each performs and the checks its output still requires
- Construct trajectory records that support bounded admission checks and independent per-tick permission decisions

:::

## Continuous Trajectory Generation {#sec-planning-continuous-trajectories}

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-opening-machine
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE MACHINE'S ARM LOOP AND CHUNK-POLICY LATENCY
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-continuous-trajectories (opening paragraph).
# │
# │ Goal:    Pin the arm tracking rate and chunk inference latency the opening
# │          quotes for the warehouse mobile manipulator.
# │ Show:    1 kHz joint loop; 40 ms P99 chunk inference; 150 ms interference tail.
# │ How:     RM registry fields; the tail is a scenario assumption.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_frequency, fmt_latency

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class PlanningOpeningMachine:
    """Arm tracking rate and chunk-policy inference latency on the machine."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    f_track = RM.arm.control_frequency  # category: datasheet; arm joint loop, registry
    t_chunk = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative; P99 incl. vision, registry
    t_tail = 150 * millisecond  # category: illustrative; interference tail

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    tail_over_nominal = (t_tail / t_chunk).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(f_track.to("hertz").magnitude - 1000.0) < 1e-9, "arm loop rate changed")
    check(abs(t_chunk.to(millisecond).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, "chunk inference latency changed")
    check(tail_over_nominal > 3, "interference tail no longer several times the nominal pass")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    f_track_str = fmt_frequency(f_track)
    t_chunk_str = fmt_latency(t_chunk, unit=millisecond)
    t_tail_str = fmt_latency(t_tail, unit=millisecond)
```

Trajectory planning converts a goal into motion a body can execute. Robotics has long posed the problem in two parts: find a collision-free path through the space of the machine's joint configurations, then assign that path a timing the actuators can follow. Physical AI changes both parts. The proposer is often a learned policy that emits short chunks of future setpoints from camera images rather than a search over a known map, and it replans continuously while the body moves, so each plan must take over from motion already under way instead of starting from rest. The inference that produces a plan takes a variable, heavy-tailed time, and the machine keeps moving throughout it. The central question is therefore broader than whether a motion avoids obstacles. A planner must also establish how long a proposed motion remains executable, how it joins the motion it replaces, and how the machine stops if its successor never arrives.

This chapter establishes those answers in the order a plan must satisfy them. It fixes what the planner hands to the tracking controller and the permission path, including the kinematic map between joint space and tool space and its damped inverse, then sizes the prediction horizon and replacement deadline against inference latency. It derives the physical limits that make a timed motion followable, from rigid-body dynamics through seam continuity and time parameterization. It then builds the jerk-limited stop that every admitted plan carries, and only after those obligations are clear compares the generators, from sampling-based search to learned action chunks, that propose candidate motion. It closes with the failures that invalidate a plan and the trajectory record that carries these obligations to the permission path.

The warehouse mobile manipulator makes the question concrete. It is reaching for a mug on a moving conveyor when its next motion proposal is delayed. The intent lease still identifies the mug, but the arm must keep moving smoothly or begin a controlled stop, and a target with an expiry time specifies neither motion. Planning must supply a timed path, a feasible transition from the motion already under way, and a stopping continuation that does not depend on the next inference finishing.

On this machine the arm's joint tracking loop evaluates feedback and setpoints at `{python} PlanningOpeningMachine.f_track_str` (datasheet; see the Reader Guide); that period does not specify the physical stopping response. Above this loop sits the Brain, where Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) [@zhao2023learning] or Diffusion Policies [@chi2024diffusionpolicy] process observations to synthesize future reference paths on the application processor.[^fn-plan-action-chunking] The machine's chunk policy is budgeted at an illustrative `{python} PlanningOpeningMachine.t_chunk_str` per pass at P99, vision included, yet memory or scheduling interference can stretch a single pass beyond `{python} PlanningOpeningMachine.t_tail_str`. The controller therefore needs both buffered nominal motion and an independently executable stop.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The kinetic energy a trajectory commits, and the stopping distance that energy demands, are derived in @sec-body-kinetic-momentum.
:::

A geometric path specifies where the arm should pass. A trajectory also specifies when it should pass each point, making velocity and acceleration available for checking against the body's limits. Geometric search, numerical optimization, and learned action chunking all propose trajectories (@sec-planning-paradigms), and every one of them faces the execution requirements below.

The learned policy remains a proposer. A downstream trajectory generator can shape its output into a timed, smooth candidate, but the independent permission path must still check that candidate before motion is admitted. A smooth reference is useful evidence for that decision; it does not establish that the motors can follow it or that the stopping clearance is sufficient.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The runtime gatekeeper that checks every admitted setpoint against live state is built in @sec-enforcement-deterministic-gatekeeper.
:::

A multi-step action chunk contains future setpoints that the tracking controller consumes while the proposer computes a replacement. Each replacement creates an **execution seam**, the junction where one chunk's setpoints give way to the next. Matching position alone can leave a velocity step, and matching velocity can still leave an acceleration step. Because the body has inertia, these changes demand abrupt forces or torques. The trajectory generator must join chunks through position, velocity, and acceleration, the continuity condition denoted by $C^2$, and then check the forces and clearance needed inside that join. The later seam derivation makes those checks explicit.

The separation of rates lets the tracking controller consume admitted references on its own clock while inference takes a variable amount of time. Buffering addresses that timing mismatch, but it cannot make the stored references valid indefinitely. The planning deadline must leave time to enter a feasible stop before either the references or their supporting evidence expire.

[^fn-plan-action-chunking]: **Action chunking representations**\index{Action chunking!architectures}\index{Policy learning!temporal horizons}: ACT and Diffusion Policy, the 2023-era chunk policies, carry no boundary-derivative constraints. Real-time chunking [@black2025realtime] conditions each new chunk on the actions already committed, which makes a consistent join more likely without guaranteeing one, so the planner still proposes a transition bridge across each replanning seam and the permission path checks it before admission.

The self-contained proposal must carry its seam state, continuous through acceleration ($C^2$),[^fn-plan-c2-spline] its deadlines, and a stopping suffix checked within clearance ($d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clear}}$). The safety microcontroller (MCU) admits that content through its independent permission path across the proposal boundary (@sec-boundary-machine-model) and keeps the stopping continuation in protected memory before it is needed.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Expiring intent leases provide the bounded time windows discharged by trajectories in @sec-intent-lease.
:::

[^fn-plan-c2-spline]: **$C^2$ derivative continuity**\index{C2 continuity@$C^2$ continuity}\index{Drivetrain!jerk dynamics}: $C^2$ continuity means that position, velocity, and acceleration remain unbroken functions of time across trajectory boundaries. In permanent-magnet synchronous motors (PMSM), electromagnetic torque couples directly to quadrature stator current ($\tau = K_t I_q$). An acceleration step asks for a finite torque and current step under this model, while a velocity step implies an ideal acceleration impulse.

Momentum, a long inference tail, and a seam that must stay continuous together decide what a plan has to contain. The first decision is therefore what the planner hands to the tracking controller and the permission path while the arm is still moving.

## The Planning Handoff and the Trajectory Record {#sec-planning-handoff}

For the reach toward the mug, the planner needs both a target and evidence of free space. It consumes the spatial belief record of @sec-memory, which supplies obstacle geometry and clearance, and the intent lease of @sec-intent, which supplies the grounded goal, task tolerances, effort ceilings, and time-bounded intent lease ($t_{\mathrm{intent\_exp}}$). The resulting motion must also respect the actuator and transmission limits of the physical body (@sec-body). The handoff connects those inputs to the checks that permit execution.

For a manipulator, a configuration $(q_1, \dots, q_n)$ is the collection of joint positions. All such configurations form the **configuration space**\index{Configuration space!definition}[^fn-configuration-space-origin] $\mathcal{C}$; removing configurations occupied by obstacles leaves $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{free}} = \mathcal{C} \setminus \mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ [@lozanoperez1983spatial]. A path through this space still lacks timing. An **executable trajectory**\index{Executable trajectory!definition} assigns physical timestamps, generating continuous state references $\mathbf{x}(t) = [\mathbf{q}(t)^T, \dot{\mathbf{q}}(t)^T, \ddot{\mathbf{q}}(t)^T]^T$ alongside feedforward torque profiles $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{ff}}(t)$. The references state the intended position, velocity, and acceleration; the feedforward terms supply the torque predicted by the model. The candidate crosses the proposal boundary for independent checking. Only admitted actuator commands can cross the causal boundary.

[^fn-configuration-space-origin]: **Configuration space**\index{Configuration space!history}: @lozanoperez1983spatial shrank the moving body to a point by growing each obstacle by the body's shape, and in the same year @schwartz1983piano treated the "piano movers' problem" as a search of exactly this space. The reduction turns a collision query into a membership test on $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{obs}}$, but the space gains a dimension with every joint, which is why collision queries dominate the run time of the sampling planners in @sec-planning-paradigms.

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-two-link-arm
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ JOINT SPACE VERSUS TOOL SPACE FOR A PLANAR TWO-LINK ARM
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-handoff (kinematics paragraph),
# │          @sec-planning-future-state-conditioning (tool displacement),
# │          @sec-planning-rigidbody-dynamics (one-joint reduction).
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that a tool-speed limit does not bound joint speed near a
# │          singularity, using the arm's published link lengths.
# │ Show:    l1 = 0.316 m, l2 = 0.384 m, reach 0.700 m; det J = l1 l2 sin q2;
# │          1.0 m/s in the weakest direction needs |qdot| = 4.90 rad/s at a
# │          90 degree elbow (one joint >= 3.46 rad/s > 2.175 rad/s) and
# │          37.8 rad/s at a 10 degree elbow.
# │ How:     Franka FER kinematic chain (d3, d5) and joint velocity limit from
# │          the registry (franka2023robot); smallest singular value of the
# │          2x2 Jacobian.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_length, fmt_angular_velocity, fmt_velocity, fmt_int

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

def _two_link_sigma_min(l1_m, l2_m, q2_deg):
    """Smallest singular value of the planar two-link Jacobian at q1 = 0 (rank depends only on q2)."""
    q2 = np.radians(q2_deg)
    jac = np.array([[-l2_m * np.sin(q2), -l2_m * np.sin(q2)], [l1_m + l2_m * np.cos(q2), l2_m * np.cos(q2)]])
    return float(np.linalg.svd(jac, compute_uv=False)[-1])

class PlanningTwoLinkArm:
    """Planar two-link abstraction of the arm: forward kinematics and Jacobian conditioning."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    l1 = RM.arm.upper_arm_length  # category: datasheet; FER DH d3, shoulder to elbow, registry (franka2023robot)
    l2 = RM.arm.forearm_length  # category: datasheet; FER DH d5, elbow to wrist, registry (franka2023robot)
    qd_max = RM.arm.joint_velocity_limits[1]  # category: datasheet; FER joints 1-4 velocity limit, registry (franka2023robot)
    v_tool = RM.tcp_speed_limit  # category: chosen; free-space TCP limit, registry
    q2_good_deg = 90  # category: illustrative; right-angle elbow
    q2_bad_deg = 10  # category: illustrative; nearly straight elbow

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    reach = (l1 + l2).to(ureg.meter)
    sig_good = _two_link_sigma_min(l1.magnitude, l2.magnitude, q2_good_deg)
    sig_bad = _two_link_sigma_min(l1.magnitude, l2.magnitude, q2_bad_deg)
    qd_norm_good = (v_tool / (sig_good * ureg.meter)).to(ureg.second**-1).magnitude * ureg.radian / ureg.second
    qd_norm_bad = (v_tool / (sig_bad * ureg.meter)).to(ureg.second**-1).magnitude * ureg.radian / ureg.second
    qd_one_good = qd_norm_good / np.sqrt(2)  # some joint must reach at least ||qdot|| / sqrt(2)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(reach.magnitude - 0.700) < 1e-12, "planar reach changed")
    check(abs(qd_norm_good.magnitude - 4.8968) < 1e-3, "right-angle joint-rate norm changed")
    check(abs(qd_norm_bad.magnitude - 37.760) < 1e-2, "near-singular joint-rate norm changed")
    check(qd_one_good > qd_max, "right-angle weakest direction no longer exceeds the joint limit")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    l1_str = fmt_length(l1, unit=ureg.meter, precision=3)
    l2_str = fmt_length(l2, unit=ureg.meter, precision=3)
    reach_str = fmt_length(reach, unit=ureg.meter, precision=2)
    qd_max_str = fmt_angular_velocity(qd_max, precision=3)
    v_tool_str = fmt_velocity(v_tool)
    q2_good_str = fmt_int(q2_good_deg)
    q2_bad_str = fmt_int(q2_bad_deg)
    qd_norm_good_str = fmt_angular_velocity(qd_norm_good, precision=1)
    qd_norm_bad_str = fmt_angular_velocity(qd_norm_bad, precision=1)
    qd_one_good_str = fmt_angular_velocity(qd_one_good, precision=1)
```

The drives track joint angles, but clearance is measured in the task space where the tool, the mug, and the conveyor guard sit. A planar two-link abstraction of the arm's shoulder, elbow, and wrist makes the map between the two spaces concrete. With upper-arm length $l_1$ and forearm length $l_2$, **forward kinematics**\index{Forward kinematics!two-link arm} gives the tool position as a function of the joint angles:

$$x = l_1\cos q_1 + l_2\cos(q_1+q_2), \qquad y = l_1\sin q_1 + l_2\sin(q_1+q_2)$$ {#eq-plan-two-link-kinematics}

Differentiating @eq-plan-two-link-kinematics gives tool velocity $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{J}(\mathbf{q})\,\dot{\mathbf{q}}$, where the **Jacobian**\index{Jacobian!manipulator}[^fn-jacobian-autograd-bridge] $\mathbf{J} = \partial\mathbf{x}/\partial\mathbf{q}$ changes with configuration. For the two-link arm its determinant is $l_1 l_2 \sin q_2$, which vanishes when the elbow straightens, the singular pose at which no joint motion moves the tool along the arm. Taking the link lengths from the arm's published kinematic chain, `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.l1_str` and `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.l2_str` for a `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.reach_str` planar reach [@franka2023robot], moving the tool at the `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.v_tool_str` TCP limit in the arm's weakest direction, the tool direction that a unit of joint rate moves least (the smallest singular value $\sigma_{\min}$ of $\mathbf{J}$, so that $\|\dot{\mathbf{q}}\| = v/\sigma_{\min}$), needs a joint-rate vector of magnitude `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_good_str` at a `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.q2_good_str`° elbow. At least one joint must then turn at `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_one_good_str`, above the published `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_max_str` limit of the shoulder and elbow joints. At a `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.q2_bad_str`° elbow the requirement grows to `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_bad_str` (@fig-11-two-link-singularity). A tool-speed limit therefore bounds no joint speed near a singularity. Every tool-space quantity this chapter checks, the TCP limit, the stopping distance, and the swept clearance, must be mapped back through $\mathbf{J}$ to the joint limits the drives enforce. The seven-joint arm has redundant joints that let a planner avoid such poses, which this planar abstraction omits.

[^fn-jacobian-autograd-bridge]: **Manipulator Jacobian**\index{Jacobian!automatic differentiation}: It is the same object automatic differentiation builds, the matrix of first derivatives of an output with respect to its inputs, here tool position with respect to joint angles. Reverse-mode autograd never forms the matrix; it computes products $\mathbf{J}^T\mathbf{v}$, and the manipulator equation uses that same transpose product to map a tool wrench into joint torques (@eq-plan-rigidbody-dynamics). A planner is the unusual consumer that must *invert* $\mathbf{J}$, and it is the inverse, not the Jacobian, that fails at a singularity.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Forward kinematics, the manipulator Jacobian, and singularities are developed in @sec-appendix-control-kinematics.
:::

::: {#fig-11-two-link-singularity fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**The same tool speed, two elbows**: The planar two-link arm drawn to scale with its `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.l1_str` and `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.l2_str` links. Each ellipse is the set of tool velocities that a unit joint-rate vector can produce, drawn at one scale in both panels; its short axis is the weakest direction (arrow). At a right-angle elbow the ellipse is round enough that `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.v_tool_str` in that direction needs `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_good_str` of joint rate. Near the straight elbow the ellipse collapses toward a line across the arm, and the same tool speed along the arm needs `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_bad_str`." fig-alt="Two panels, each showing a two-link arm drawn from a shoulder joint through an elbow joint to a tool point, with a dashed arc marking the arm's reach. In the left panel the elbow is bent at a right angle and a wide shaded ellipse surrounds the tool point, with a double arrow along its short axis. In the right panel the arm is nearly straight, the tool sits near the reach arc, and the ellipse is a thin sliver across the arm with the double arrow pointing along the arm. Text in each panel gives the joint rate needed for 1 meter per second along the arrow: 4.9 and 37.8 radians per second."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-planning-two-link-singularity
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TWO-LINK ARM AT TWO ELBOW ANGLES (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-11-two-link-singularity in @sec-planning-continuous-trajectories.
# │
# │ Goal:    Make the Jacobian's conditioning visible: the same tool speed costs
# │          little joint rate at a right-angle elbow and much more near straight.
# │ Show:    the arm to scale at q2 = 90 and 10 degrees; the tool-velocity
# │          ellipse J * (unit joint-rate circle); the weakest direction.
# │ How:     PlanningTwoLinkArm link lengths, elbow angles, TCP limit, and
# │          joint-rate norms; the guard ties the drawn ellipses to the cell.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import viz
import numpy as np

TL = PlanningTwoLinkArm
R = viz.VOL4_ROLES
l1, l2 = TL.l1.to(ureg.meter).magnitude, TL.l2.to(ureg.meter).magnitude
v_tool = TL.v_tool.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second).magnitude
k_ell = 0.25  # drawing scale: meters of page per (m/s) of tool speed

def _jac(q1, q2):
    return np.array(
        [[-l1 * np.sin(q1) - l2 * np.sin(q1 + q2), -l2 * np.sin(q1 + q2)], [l1 * np.cos(q1) + l2 * np.cos(q1 + q2), l2 * np.cos(q1 + q2)]]
    )

cases = [(TL.q2_good_deg, TL.qd_norm_good), (TL.q2_bad_deg, TL.qd_norm_bad)]
viz.set_book_style()
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.4, 3.1))
drawn = []
for ax, tag, (q2d, qd_need) in zip(axes, ("a", "b"), cases):
    q2 = np.radians(q2d)
    q1 = np.radians(45) - np.arctan2(l2 * np.sin(q2), l1 + l2 * np.cos(q2))  # tool direction at 45 degrees
    elbow = np.array([l1 * np.cos(q1), l1 * np.sin(q1)])
    tool = elbow + l2 * np.array([np.cos(q1 + q2), np.sin(q1 + q2)])
    # reach circle
    arc = np.radians(np.linspace(-14, 80, 120))
    th = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200)
    ax.plot(TL.reach.magnitude * np.cos(arc), TL.reach.magnitude * np.sin(arc), color=R["neutral"], lw=0.6, ls=(0, (3, 3)))
    # links
    ax.plot([0, elbow[0], tool[0]], [0, elbow[1], tool[1]], color=R["structural"], lw=3.2, solid_capstyle="round", zorder=3)
    for p in ((0, 0), elbow):
        ax.plot(*p, "o", ms=6.5, mfc="white", mec=R["structural"], mew=1.4, zorder=4)
    ax.plot(*tool, "o", ms=3.5, color=R["structural"], zorder=4)
    # velocity ellipse: image of the unit joint-rate circle, scaled so the tool speed per (rad/s)
    J = _jac(q1, q2)
    U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(J)
    circ = np.vstack([np.cos(th), np.sin(th)])
    ell = (J @ circ) * k_ell
    ax.fill(tool[0] + ell[0], tool[1] + ell[1], color=R["measured"], alpha=0.14, lw=0, zorder=2)
    ax.plot(tool[0] + ell[0], tool[1] + ell[1], color=R["measured"], lw=1.0, zorder=2)
    # weakest direction
    u_min = U[:, 1]
    ax.annotate("", xy=tool + u_min * 0.13, xytext=tool - u_min * 0.13, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=R["proposal"], lw=1.2), zorder=5)
    drawn.append((s[1], qd_need.magnitude))
    ax.text(0.0, 1.0, f"({tag}) elbow {q2d}°", transform=ax.transAxes, ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=R["neutral"])
    ax.text(
        0.97,
        0.03,
        f"weakest direction:\n{v_tool:g} m/s needs {qd_need.magnitude:.1f} rad/s",
        transform=ax.transAxes,
        ha="right",
        va="bottom",
        fontsize=8.5,
        color=R["proposal"],
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="square,pad=0.1", fc="white", ec="none"),
    )
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xlim(-0.12, 0.82)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.22, 0.74)
    ax.axis("off")
    ax.text(0.03, -0.035, "shoulder", fontsize=8, color=R["neutral"], ha="left", va="top")
axes[0].text(
    TL.reach.magnitude * np.cos(np.radians(12)) + 0.035,
    TL.reach.magnitude * np.sin(np.radians(12)),
    f"reach\n{TL.reach.magnitude:.2f} m",
    fontsize=8,
    color=R["neutral"],
    ha="left",
    va="center",
)
check(
    abs(drawn[0][1] - v_tool / drawn[0][0]) < 1e-6 and abs(drawn[1][1] - v_tool / drawn[1][0]) < 1e-6,
    "Two-link figure: drawn ellipse minor axes must give the cell's joint-rate norms.",
)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-dls-step
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ONE DAMPED-LEAST-SQUARES INVERSE-KINEMATICS STEP ON THE TWO-LINK ARM
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-handoff (inverse-kinematics paragraphs after
# │          @fig-11-two-link-singularity).
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that damping bounds the joint command near the singularity
# │          the figure shows, and what it costs in tool motion.
# │ Show:    lambda = 50 mm; weakest-direction 1.0 m/s request needs 4.6 rad/s
# │          (was 4.9) at a 90 degree elbow, 94.3 percent of the request realized;
# │          8.3 rad/s (was 37.8) at a 10 degree elbow, 21.9 percent realized;
# │          bound v / (2 lambda) = 10 rad/s at any configuration.
# │ How:     Per singular direction the DLS gain is sigma / (sigma^2 + lambda^2)
# │          and the realized fraction sigma^2 / (sigma^2 + lambda^2)
# │          (wampler1986manipulator; nakamura1986inverse); sigma_min from
# │          PlanningTwoLinkArm. Chapter-local: promote to MLSysIM only if a
# │          second chapter reuses it.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_length, fmt_angular_velocity, fmt_percent

class PlanningDLSStep:
    """Damped-least-squares IK gain and realized tool motion in the arm's weakest direction."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    lam = 50 * ureg.millimeter  # category: chosen; illustrative damping, not a vendor setting
    v_tool = PlanningTwoLinkArm.v_tool  # category: chosen; free-space TCP limit, registry
    qd_max = PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_max  # category: datasheet; shoulder and elbow limit, registry
    sig_good = PlanningTwoLinkArm.sig_good * ureg.meter  # derived; 90 degree elbow
    sig_bad = PlanningTwoLinkArm.sig_bad * ureg.meter  # derived; 10 degree elbow

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    def _gain(sig, lam):
        return (sig / (sig**2 + lam**2)).to(ureg.meter**-1)

    def _realized(sig, lam):
        return (sig**2 / (sig**2 + lam**2)).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    rad_s = ureg.radian / ureg.second
    qd_dls_good = (v_tool * _gain(sig_good, lam)).to(ureg.second**-1).magnitude * rad_s
    qd_dls_bad = (v_tool * _gain(sig_bad, lam)).to(ureg.second**-1).magnitude * rad_s
    qd_bound = (v_tool / (2 * lam)).to(ureg.second**-1).magnitude * rad_s
    frac_good = _realized(sig_good, lam)
    frac_bad = _realized(sig_bad, lam)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(qd_dls_good < PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_good, "damping must not raise the joint command")
    check(qd_dls_bad < PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_bad / 4, "damping no longer cuts the near-singular command by 4x")
    check(qd_dls_bad <= qd_bound and qd_dls_good <= qd_bound, "DLS gain exceeded its 1/(2 lambda) bound")
    check(abs(qd_bound.magnitude - 10.0) < 1e-9, "DLS joint-rate bound changed")
    check(frac_good > 0.9 and frac_bad < 0.3, "damping no longer spares the good pose and taxes the bad one")
    check(qd_dls_bad > qd_max, "damped command now within the joint limit; revise the feasibility sentence")
    # margin_dls_joint_rate_knee.svg fig-alt hand-types 4.9, 37.8, 4.6, 8.3 and 10 rad/s.
    check(
        [round(PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_good.magnitude, 1), round(PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_bad.magnitude, 1),
         round(qd_dls_good.magnitude, 1), round(qd_dls_bad.magnitude, 1)] == [4.9, 37.8, 4.6, 8.3],
        "DLS knee margin fig-alt values are stale",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    lam_str = fmt_length(lam, unit=ureg.millimeter)
    qd_dls_good_str = fmt_angular_velocity(qd_dls_good, precision=1)
    qd_dls_bad_str = fmt_angular_velocity(qd_dls_bad, precision=1)
    qd_bound_str = fmt_angular_velocity(qd_bound, precision=0)
    frac_good_str = fmt_percent(frac_good, precision=1, style="prose")
    frac_bad_str = fmt_percent(frac_bad, precision=1, style="prose")
```

The same map must also run in reverse. A proposal stated in tool space, whether a grasp pose from the intent lease or a Cartesian velocity from a policy or a teleoperation device, leaves the planner to find the joint motion that produces it, the **inverse kinematics**\index{Inverse kinematics!differential step} problem. The two-link arm has a closed-form inverse, but a seven-joint arm replanning chunk by chunk is solved by differential steps: linearize at the current configuration and solve $\mathbf{J}\,\Delta\mathbf{q} = \Delta\mathbf{x}$ for the joint step that moves the tool by $\Delta\mathbf{x}$, then repeat from the new configuration. Where $\mathbf{J}$ is invertible the exact step is $\Delta\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{J}^{-1}\Delta\mathbf{x}$. Written along the singular directions of $\mathbf{J}$, this step divides the part of $\Delta\mathbf{x}$ along each tool direction by that direction's singular value $\sigma$. The weakest direction therefore receives the largest joint step, $1/\sigma_{\min}$ per unit of tool motion, which is exactly the joint-rate demand that @fig-11-two-link-singularity shows growing without bound as the elbow straightens. An exact inverse passes the singularity's arithmetic straight to the drives.

**Damped least squares**\index{Damped least squares!inverse kinematics} gives up exactness to bound the step [@wampler1986manipulator; @nakamura1986inverse]. Instead of demanding $\mathbf{J}\,\Delta\mathbf{q} = \Delta\mathbf{x}$, it chooses the joint step that best trades tool error against joint motion, with a damping length $\lambda$ that sets the exchange rate:

$$\Delta\mathbf{q}_\lambda = \arg\min_{\Delta\mathbf{q}} \left(\|\mathbf{J}\,\Delta\mathbf{q}-\Delta\mathbf{x}\|^2 + \lambda^2\|\Delta\mathbf{q}\|^2\right) = \mathbf{J}^T\!\left(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{J}^T+\lambda^2\mathbf{I}\right)^{-1}\Delta\mathbf{x}$$ {#eq-plan-dls-ik}

Setting the gradient of the objective to zero gives $(\mathbf{J}^T\mathbf{J}+\lambda^2\mathbf{I})\,\Delta\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{J}^T\Delta\mathbf{x}$, and moving $\mathbf{J}^T$ through the inverse yields the form in @eq-plan-dls-ik, which needs only a $2 \times 2$ solve for the planar arm. A reader who has trained a model will recognize ridge regression, with $\lambda^2$ as the weight-decay coefficient. Along each singular direction the gain changes from $1/\sigma$ to $\sigma/(\sigma^2+\lambda^2)$. Far from the singularity, where $\sigma \gg \lambda$, the two agree. As $\sigma$ falls toward zero the damped gain falls with it instead of diverging, and it never exceeds $1/(2\lambda)$, reached where $\sigma = \lambda$. The damping thus places a configuration-independent ceiling on the joint step, which no choice of pose can breach.

With an illustrative $\lambda$ of `{python} PlanningDLSStep.lam_str`, the weakest-direction request at the `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.v_tool_str` TCP limit needs `{python} PlanningDLSStep.qd_dls_good_str` of joint rate at the `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.q2_good_str`° elbow, against `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_good_str` undamped, and the tool still realizes `{python} PlanningDLSStep.frac_good_str` of the requested motion. At the `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.q2_bad_str`° elbow the damped command is `{python} PlanningDLSStep.qd_dls_bad_str` instead of `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_bad_str`, and no pose can demand more than `{python} PlanningDLSStep.qd_bound_str`. The price is paid where the damping acts: the tool realizes only `{python} PlanningDLSStep.frac_bad_str` of the requested motion along the arm, so the step lags its target in exactly the direction the arm cannot move well. That residual is a tracking error the planner must carry into the trajectory's timing and clearance checks rather than discard. A larger $\lambda$ lowers the ceiling and enlarges the error everywhere, which is why practical solvers raise the damping only as $\sigma_{\min}$ approaches it.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_dls_joint_rate_knee.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Joint-rate norm needed for 1 meter per second in the weakest direction, plotted on a log scale against elbow angle from 90 degrees down to near straight. The exact-inverse curve climbs steeply from 4.9 at 90 degrees to 37.8 radians per second at 10 degrees. The damped curve stays below a dashed ceiling at 10 radians per second, reading 4.6 and 8.3 at the same two elbows."}

*As the elbow straightens, the exact inverse climbs from `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_good_str` to `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_bad_str`; damping caps it at `{python} PlanningDLSStep.qd_bound_str`.*
:::

Damping bounds the inverse-kinematics step; it does not make the step feasible. Even the damped `{python} PlanningDLSStep.qd_dls_bad_str` exceeds the `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_max_str` joint limit, so the planner must still slow the tool through time parameterization (@sec-planning-time-parameterization), and the permission path still checks every joint rate against the limits the drives enforce. Damped least squares is a better proposal, not a permission. The general $n$-joint form, with its singular-value expansion, is stated in @sec-appendix-control-kinematics.

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-lease-rule
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ONE CHUNK LEASE FOR BOTH BODIES: THE ARM'S LEASE PATH AND ALTERNATE CUTOFF
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-handoff (TRACK/STOP paragraph),
# │          @sec-planning-behavior-seam (arm lease path),
# │          @sec-planning-trajectory-contract (record expiry, filled record).
# │
# │ Goal:    Charge the arm's stop from the last admitted chunk when the
# │          shared chunk lease lapses; separately derive the alternate cutoff.
# │ Show:    60 ms lease, renewed every 50 ms; lease path 60 + 1 + 1 + 20 =
# │          82 ms, 82 mm at 1.0 m/s; with the 137.5 mm S-curve stop (275 ms),
# │          219.5 mm of 300 mm, leaving 80.5 mm; alternate path leaves
# │          102.5 mm from its later epoch; alternate admission cutoff
# │          300 - 22 = 278 ms from schedule origin.
# │ How:     AISLE lease, tick, bus, and brake onset (charged as the arm's
# │          onset, conservative); RM TCP limit; the arm's jerk bound is the
# │          peak jerk of the reference C2 polynomial at the same peak
# │          (calc_c2_stop_suffix), and the stop is calc_scurve_stop_distance
# │          / calc_scurve_stop_time. The arm's worked deadlines and clearance
# │          are defined here and read by calc-planning-arm-timeline and
# │          calc-planning-c2-stop-clearance.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg, millisecond
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class PlanningLeaseRule:
    """The arm lease path and the alternate schedule admission cutoff."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen; chunk lease (@sec-nervous-cadences), registry
    f_renew = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen; admitted-chunk renewal rate, registry
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: derived; permission-loop period, registry
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative; fieldbus cycle, registry
    t_onset = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative; brake onset, charged as the arm's onset
    v_arm = RM.tcp_speed_limit  # category: chosen; free-space TCP limit, registry
    t_blend = 240 * millisecond  # category: chosen; blend deadline
    t_commit = 300 * millisecond  # category: chosen; physical suffix onset
    a_arm_stop = 5.0 * ureg.meter / ureg.second**2  # category: illustrative; arm stop deceleration bound
    d_arm_clear = 300 * ureg.millimeter  # category: illustrative; obstacle clearance

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    t_renew = (1 / f_renew).to(millisecond)
    t_lease_slack = (t_lease - t_renew).to(millisecond)
    t_dispatch = (t_tick + t_bus + t_onset).to(millisecond)
    t_lease_path = (t_lease + t_dispatch).to(millisecond)
    d_lease_path = (v_arm * t_lease_path).to(ureg.millimeter)
    j_arm_stop = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_arm, a_arm_stop)["peak_jerk"]  # jerk bound: reference polynomial's peak
    t_arm_stop = calc_scurve_stop_time(v_arm, a_arm_stop, j_arm_stop).to(millisecond)
    arm_stop_dist = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_arm, a_arm_stop, j_arm_stop).to(ureg.millimeter)
    lease_total = d_lease_path + arm_stop_dist
    lease_margin = d_arm_clear - lease_total
    commit_margin = d_arm_clear - (v_arm * (t_commit - t_blend)).to(ureg.millimeter) - arm_stop_dist
    t_alt_admission_cutoff = (t_commit - t_dispatch).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(t_lease.to(millisecond).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "chunk lease changed")
    check(abs(t_renew.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "renewal period changed")
    check(t_renew < t_lease, "lease no longer outlasts one renewal period")
    check(abs(t_lease_slack.magnitude - 10.0) < 1e-9, "lease slack beyond one renewal period changed")
    check(abs(t_lease_path.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, "arm lease path changed")
    check(abs(d_lease_path.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, "arm lease-path travel changed")
    check(abs(j_arm_stop.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second**3).magnitude - 200.0 / 3.0) < 1e-9, "arm jerk bound changed")
    check(abs(t_arm_stop.magnitude - 275.0) < 1e-9, "arm S-curve stop duration changed")
    check(abs(arm_stop_dist.magnitude - 137.5) < 1e-9, "arm S-curve stop distance changed")
    check(abs(lease_total.magnitude - 219.5) < 1e-9, "arm lease-path stop total changed")
    check(abs(lease_margin.magnitude - 80.5) < 1e-9, "arm lease-path margin changed")
    check(abs(commit_margin.magnitude - 102.5) < 1e-9, "arm commitment-path margin changed")
    check(abs(t_dispatch.magnitude - 22.0) < 1e-9, "tick + bus + onset changed")
    check(abs(t_alt_admission_cutoff.magnitude - 278.0) < 1e-9, "alternate admission cutoff changed")
    check(lease_total <= d_arm_clear, "running lease-path stop exceeds illustrative clearance")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease, unit=millisecond)
    t_renew_str = fmt_latency(t_renew, unit=millisecond)
    t_lease_slack_str = fmt_latency(t_lease_slack, unit=millisecond)
    t_dispatch_str = fmt_latency(t_dispatch, unit=millisecond)
    t_lease_path_str = fmt_latency(t_lease_path, unit=millisecond)
    d_lease_path_str = fmt_length(d_lease_path, unit=ureg.millimeter)
    v_arm_str = fmt_velocity(v_arm)
    arm_stop_dist_str = fmt_length(arm_stop_dist, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    lease_total_str = fmt_length(lease_total, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    lease_margin_str = fmt_length(lease_margin, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    commit_margin_str = fmt_length(commit_margin, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    d_arm_clear_str = fmt_length(d_arm_clear, unit=ureg.millimeter)
    t_alt_admission_cutoff_str = fmt_latency(t_alt_admission_cutoff, unit=millisecond)
```

What the planner hands over is a **trajectory record**\index{Trajectory record!definition}, the ninth record in the record chain and the immutable proposal that the tracking controller follows and the permission path admits. Consuming the geometric obstacle bounds from the spatial belief record and the task target and lease window from the intent lease, the trajectory record binds unprivileged neural sequence predictions to certified physical invariants. In the systems architecture, the trajectory record serves as the formal boundary between the unprivileged, asynchronous Brain and the deterministic, hard real-time Nervous System. It names its coordinate frame $\mathcal{F}$, evidence time $t_0$, initial reference state, and four deadlines defined in the **MCU monotonic clock domain**: nominal tracking begins at $t_{\mathrm{start}}$, the nominal setpoints end at $t_{\mathrm{plan\_exp}}$, the matched stop must physically begin at $t_{\mathrm{commit}}$, and the admitted stop finishes at $t_{\mathrm{stop\_end}}$. It also links to the active intent lease expiry $t_{\mathrm{intent\_exp}}$. Conversion from host and sensor timestamps carries a bounded synchronization error. The planner schedules each replacement against an earlier internal milestone, the blend deadline $t_{\mathrm{blend}}$, by which a preferred successor should clear validation; it is an internal scheduling target rather than an exposed record field. The latest replacement-admission decision precedes physical stop onset by the reserved decision, transport, and actuator delay. The example below distinguishes these events explicitly.

The permission path permits nominal **TRACK** only while the intent lease and trajectory record remain valid, so an expired intent lease terminates nominal tracking immediately, regardless of what the trajectory's own timestamps allow. To manage asynchronous inference latency tails and hardware faults without compromising safety, the architecture enforces a strict **two-tier deadline hierarchy**:

1.  **Fast Nervous System periodic chunk lease ($t_{\mathrm{lease}}$, `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str`):** This high-rate heartbeat governs the real-time execution contract between Brain and Nervous System. The chunk policy proposes base velocity and arm joint targets together, so one chunk lease (@sec-nervous-cadences) governs both bodies, and only an admitted replacement chunk renews it, with a desired admission interval of `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_renew_str` on this machine. Qualification must bound successful-admission interarrival, not merely inference or request cadence. If an upstream inference pass hangs or communication drops, the lease lapses `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_slack_str` after its expected renewal, immediately requesting a controlled stop whose onset follows the reserved response delay.
2.  **Trajectory commitment deadline:** The record names the latest physical onset of its matched stop. Replacement admission must close early enough to dispatch that stop and absorb actuator response delay. This geometric limit does not replace the running machine's shorter chunk lease; the later worked timeline examines an explicitly different, longer-lease configuration.

Two stopping responses back these deadlines. A matched stop suffix, latched at admission, begins at $t_{\mathrm{commit}}$ if no successor has been admitted; a state-matched fallback, built from the measured state, answers any earlier invalidation, such as a lapsed lease (@sec-planning-two-tier-deadlines). Either stop remains authorized after nominal tracking expires, provided its own state, clearance, sensing, and drive-energy premises still hold.

The two execution consumers read distinct subsets of the trajectory record. The downstream tracking controller interpolates admitted setpoints, timestamps, and feedforward torque terms to drive the motor inverters along a continuous profile fetched from the real-time execution jitter buffer. Simultaneously, the independent permission path inspects the record's lineage, timing bounds, dynamic assumptions, validity envelopes, and certified stopping continuation ($d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clear}}$). The permission path monitors current limits and physical tracking error on every millisecond tick without inheriting the planner's feasibility claim as proof: an unmodeled obstacle, payload slip, or contact wrench immediately revokes TRACK authority and activates the state-matched fallback. Because every contract field maps to an explicit hardware or software gate, the Nervous System safely executes fast physical motion without presuming that subsequent neural inference cycles will complete on schedule. Producing such a record begins from a goal whose validity is timed but whose motion is not yet specified.

## Trajectory Synthesis from Discrete Goals {#sec-planning-goal-to-trajectory}

The intent lease for the mug grants a goal region and effort ceilings (@sec-intent-lease), but no actuator can execute a region. The planner must choose a route, assign motion along it, and return a replacement before the current record loses tracking authority. Different synthesis methods address different parts of this task. Their outputs all face the same requirements for timing, continuous seams, and stopping clearance.

### Action chunk horizon sizing and reactive lag trade-offs {#sec-planning-horizon-tradeoff}

Before sizing the temporal prediction horizon $H$, the systems engineer must construct an end-to-end latency budget for the replacement pipeline. Trajectory replacement is not an instantaneous inference pass; it comprises a multi-stage data transport and verification sequence across the host processor and microcontroller.

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-replacement-ledger
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ REPLACEMENT-LATENCY STAGE LEDGER FOR THE MACHINE'S CHUNK POLICY
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-horizon-tradeoff (replacement-latency paragraph),
# │          @eq-plan-replacement-latency; rows 1 + 2 of @tbl-04-event-ledger.
# │
# │ Goal:    Read replacement latency L as capture to admission from the
# │          shared ledger, not from a stage list of this chapter's own.
# │ Show:    L = t_age 51.6 + Delta_da 63.3 = 114.9 ms; inside Delta_da the
# │          40 ms inference and the 18 ms whole-plan validation.
# │ How:     AISLE.perception_age (Ch8), AISLE.t_dispatch_to_admission (Ch13),
# │          AISLE.t_capture_to_admission (MLSysIM). 2026-09-29: replaced the
# │          15 + 5 + 40 + 2 + 18 + 1 = 81 ms chapter-local ledger, whose
# │          sensing stages disagreed with the registry's capture-to-dispatch age.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_latency

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class PlanningReplacementLedger:
    """Replacement latency L: capture to admission, from the two registry intervals."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age  # category: derived; capture to dispatch (@sec-perception-latency-waterfall)
    t_da = AISLE.t_dispatch_to_admission  # category: derived; dispatch to admission allocation (@sec-placement-isolation-decisions)
    t_infer = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative; P99 incl. vision, registry (inside t_da)
    t_validate = AISLE.t_plan_validate  # category: illustrative; whole-plan validation, registry (inside t_da)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    t_sum = AISLE.t_capture_to_admission.to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(t_infer.to(millisecond).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, "chunk inference latency changed")
    check(abs((t_age + t_da - t_sum).to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "L must be capture-to-dispatch plus dispatch-to-admission")
    check(abs(t_sum.magnitude - 114.91072) < 1e-6, "replacement latency changed")
    check(t_validate < t_da, "validation is counted once, inside Delta_da")
    # margin_replacement_latency_envelope.svg fig-alt hand-types 51.6, 114.9, 50 and 60 ms.
    check(
        [round(t_age.to(millisecond).magnitude, 1), round(t_sum.magnitude, 1),
         round(PlanningLeaseRule.t_renew.magnitude), round(PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease.to(millisecond).magnitude)]
        == [51.6, 114.9, 50, 60],
        "replacement-latency margin fig-alt values are stale",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(t_age.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_da_str = fmt_latency(t_da.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_infer_str = fmt_latency(t_infer, unit=millisecond)
    t_validate_str = fmt_latency(t_validate, unit=millisecond)
    t_sum_str = fmt_latency(t_sum, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

The scheduling quantity is **replacement latency**\index{Replacement latency!definition} $L$: elapsed time from the capture of the observation a new proposal rests on to the admission of that proposal. In the event vocabulary of @tbl-04-event-ledger, $L$ runs from capture to admission, so it is the sum of two intervals that other chapters derive, the capture-to-dispatch age $t_{\text{age}}$ of @sec-perception-latency-waterfall and the dispatch-to-admission interval $\Delta_{\text{da}}$ that @sec-placement-isolation-decisions allocates:
$$L = \underbrace{t_{\text{age}}}_{\text{capture}\,\to\,\text{dispatch}} + \underbrace{\Delta_{\text{da}}}_{\text{dispatch}\,\to\,\text{admission}}, \qquad \Delta_{\text{da}} = t_{\text{infer}} + t_{\text{link}} + t_{\text{deser}} + t_{\text{validate}} + t_{\text{activate}} + t_{\text{wait}}$$ {#eq-plan-replacement-latency}
On the running machine the observation is `{python} PlanningReplacementLedger.t_age_str` old at dispatch. The allocation of $\Delta_{\text{da}}$, `{python} PlanningReplacementLedger.t_da_str`, charges the chunk policy's `{python} PlanningReplacementLedger.t_infer_str` inference in full, `{python} PlanningReplacementLedger.t_validate_str` of whole-plan validation, and the board link, deserialization, activation, and wait for the next permission tick, which brings $L$ to `{python} PlanningReplacementLedger.t_sum_str`. Charging the whole inference after dispatch counts its vision stage twice, since that stage already lies in $t_{\text{age}}$, so the allocated $L$ is conservative. When stages overlap or share contention, a sum of stage percentiles is not a percentile of the sum (@sec-body-measurement-freshness), so the horizon is sized from the end-to-end distribution of $L$ measured between capture and admission timestamps.

Validation is the planner's own term in that sum. The `{python} PlanningReplacementLedger.t_validate_str` allowance is a separate admission workload, not work silently placed inside a millisecond permission tick. Admission needs bounded staging memory, the candidate and stop coefficients, and qualified local clearance evidence; the host's full scene map need not reside on the MCU. Scheduling must preserve per-tick enforcement while admission proceeds and refresh the seam check before activation. @Sec-placement must allocate and qualify that work and memory under interference. Every term is an illustrative allocation, so neither $L$ nor its parts are measured bounds; both intervals remain explicit qualification obligations.

Prediction length and execution length are separate choices. A prediction horizon $H\Delta t$ describes how far the proposer looks ahead; the **executed prefix**\index{Executed prefix!definition} is the portion used before a checked replacement takes over. Increasing the predicted horizon supplies candidate motion beyond the next renewal, but does not grant permission to execute all of it. The running machine still targets admitted renewal every `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_renew_str`, with expiry at `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str` after the last admission. Target evidence can expire sooner.

Compute amortization depends on how often inference runs, not merely on how many future setpoints it returns. Executing a longer prefix can reduce request frequency, but also delays task correction from new observations. Predicting farther while preserving the same renewal cadence does not by itself reduce inference duty. Protective response remains governed by the independent permission path and its measured response delay. Horizon selection therefore compares useful task performance, renewal throughput, evidence age, and fallback frequency under the declared workload; no universal optimal horizon follows from buffer length alone.

### Tail latency budgeting and the mission exposure wall {#sec-planning-tail-latency-budgeting}

A late replacement reduces uninterrupted task service when the resident fallback works as specified. It becomes a physical hazard only if the fallback is infeasible, unavailable, or itself delayed beyond its budget. Repeated handoffs make tail latency important for availability[^fn-tail-scale-fanout] even when each individual miss is contained; the mission calculation below quantifies deadline exposure, not collision probability.

[^fn-tail-scale-fanout]: **Tail at scale**\index{Tail latency!fan-out}: @dean2013tail showed that a request fanned out to many servers waits for the slowest of them, so a delay that is rare on each server becomes common for the request as a whole. A mission of handoffs is the same fan-out laid out in time. Every handoff must arrive, so the mission inherits the worst of them, and a per-handoff $P_{99}$ says almost nothing about whether all of them arrive.

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-mission-exposure
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MISSION EXPOSURE OF A P99 REPLACEMENT BUDGET
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-goal-to-trajectory (design-tail paragraph),
# │          chk-plan-action-chunk-horizon-tail.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show why a per-handoff P99 budget says little about a mission, and
# │          derive the per-handoff design-tail target by the union bound.
# │ Show:    K = 600 s x 5 Hz = 3000; 30 late; 0.99^3000 ~ 8e-14;
# │          1e-3 / 3000 ~ 3.3e-7, i.e. P99.99997.
# │ How:     Generic replanner (not the machine's 20 Hz chunk renewal);
# │          independence assumed, as the prose states.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_frequency, fmt_math, sci_latex

class PlanningMissionExposure:
    """Handoff count, late-handoff exposure, and union-bound design target."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    t_mission = 600 * second  # category: illustrative; ten-minute mission
    f_replan = 5 * ureg.hertz  # category: illustrative; generic replanner rate
    p_late = 0.01  # category: definitional; exceedance of a P99 budget
    eps_mission = 1e-3  # category: chosen; mission exceedance target

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    n_handoff = round((t_mission * f_replan).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    n_late = n_handoff * p_late
    p_all = (1 - p_late) ** n_handoff
    eps_handoff = eps_mission / n_handoff
    q_pct = 100 * (1 - eps_handoff)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(n_handoff == 3000, "handoff count changed")
    check(abs(n_late - 30) < 1e-9, "expected late handoffs changed")
    check(7e-14 < p_all < 9e-14, "all-on-time probability changed")
    check(abs(eps_handoff - eps_mission / 3000) < 1e-15, "per-handoff target changed")
    # margin_handoff_exceedance_ladder.svg fig-alt hand-types 0.01, 0.001 and 3.3e-7.
    check(p_late == 0.01 and eps_mission == 1e-3 and f"{eps_handoff:.1e}" == "3.3e-07", "exceedance-ladder margin fig-alt values are stale")
    check(f"{q_pct:.5f}" == "99.99997", "exceedance-ladder caption quantile P99.99997 out of date")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    f_replan_str = fmt_frequency(f_replan)
    t_mission_str = fmt_latency(t_mission, unit=second)
    n_handoff_str = fmt_int(n_handoff, commas=False)
    n_late_str = fmt_int(n_late)
    p_late_math = fmt_math(f"p={fmt(p_late, precision=2)}")
    eps_mission_math = fmt_math(rf"\epsilon_{{\mathrm{{mission}}}}={sci_latex(eps_mission, precision=0)}")
    late_math = fmt_math(rf"Kp={n_handoff}\times{fmt(p_late, precision=2)}={fmt_int(n_late)}")
    eps_ratio_math = fmt_math(rf"{fmt(p_late, precision=2)}/({sci_latex(eps_handoff, precision=1)})\approx{sci_latex(p_late / eps_handoff, precision=0)}")
    k_math = fmt_math(f"K={n_handoff}")
    p_all_math = fmt_math(rf"(0.99)^{{{n_handoff}}}\approx{sci_latex(p_all, precision=0)}")
    eps_math = fmt_math(rf"\epsilon\le\epsilon_{{\mathrm{{mission}}}}/K\approx{sci_latex(eps_handoff, precision=1)}")
    q_math = fmt_math(rf"P_{{{fmt(q_pct, precision=5, commas=False)}}}")
```

The component sum in @eq-plan-replacement-latency is an elapsed replacement path, not an absolute timestamp, and its tail matters because a mission repeats it. A mission of $K$ handoffs fails its timing target if any one of them is late. Allocating a mission exceedance target $\epsilon_{\mathrm{mission}}$ equally across the handoffs bounds the exceedance each may have, by the union bound:

$$\epsilon \le \frac{\epsilon_{\mathrm{mission}}}{K}$$ {#eq-plan-union-bound}

::: {#nbk-planning-handoff-exposure-wall .callout-notebook title="The handoff exposure wall"}

**Problem**: A generic replanner, slower than this machine's chunk renewal, meets a $P_{99}$ replacement budget on each handoff. Over a ten-minute mission, how likely is it that every handoff arrives on time, and what per-handoff tail must the design target instead?

**Variables**:

- Mission length `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.t_mission_str` and replanning rate `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.f_replan_str` (illustrative)
- Per-handoff exceedance of the $P_{99}$ budget, `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.p_late_math` (definitional)
- Mission exceedance target `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.eps_mission_math` (chosen)
- Independent misses (assumption)

**Math**:

1. **Handoff count**: `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.t_mission_str` $\times$ `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.f_replan_str` gives `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.k_math`, and `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.late_math` handoffs are expected late.
2. **Every handoff on time**: `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.p_all_math`.
3. **Design tail** (@eq-plan-union-bound): `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.eps_math`, the `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.q_math` quantile, deeper than the $P_{99}$ budget by `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.eps_ratio_math`.

**Result**: A mission almost never completes with every handoff inside a $P_{99}$ budget, and the tail a mission target implies lies more than four orders of magnitude deeper.

**Systems insight**: The quantile a design must target is set by how many handoffs a mission makes, not by the per-handoff budget, and it lies beyond what a test campaign of practical size observes. A late handoff must therefore cost service, never clearance. What keeps $d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clear}}$ is the resident stop, the matched stop suffix latched in the MCU's memory at admission and executable without the proposer, not the latency tail.

:::

The per-handoff quantile is a **design quantile target**\index{Design quantile target!definition}, a risk allocation rather than an observed latency. Correlated contention clusters misses, which breaks the independence this arithmetic assumes. A deployment either supports the target with representative load testing and a conservative bound, or accepts a higher fallback rate.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_handoff_exceedance_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Three horizontal bars on a log scale of exceedance probability per handoff: the P99 budget at 0.01, the mission target at 0.001, and the per-handoff design target at 3.3 times 10 to the minus 7."}

*Spread over `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.n_handoff_str` handoffs, a mission target demands a `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.q_math` deadline, far past $P_{99}$.*
:::

The next request leaves no later than $T_{\mathrm{request}}$ after the active chunk starts. Admission must finish before the decision cutoff that precedes $t_{\mathrm{commit}}$ by the physical response allowance, not merely before the last nominal setpoint. With a replacement-latency target $Q_{1-\epsilon}(L)$ and reserve $T_{\mathrm{reserve}}$, require $t_{\mathrm{commit}}-t_{\mathrm{start}}\ge T_{\mathrm{request}}+Q_{1-\epsilon}(L)+T_{\mathrm{reserve}}$. Here $T_{\mathrm{reserve}}$ must cover the decision-to-onset allowance as well as any scheduling reserve. The admitted stop then needs another $T_{\mathrm{stop}}$ under MCU authority. The complete **time horizon** $T_{\mathrm{record}}$ that the record must cover, regardless of encoding, has the lower bound:

$$T_{\mathrm{record}}\ge T_{\mathrm{request}}+Q_{1-\epsilon}(L)+T_{\mathrm{reserve}}+T_{\mathrm{stop}}$$ {#eq-plan-action-chunk-horizon}

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-arm-timeline
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ AUTHORITY TIMELINE FOR THE CONVEYOR-TRACKING ARM
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-goal-to-trajectory (horizon paragraph, evidence
# │          age), @sec-planning-behavior-seam (arm case).
# │
# │ Goal:    Hold the arm's timeline inputs in one place so the horizon bound,
# │          the evidence-age check, the C2 arm case, and the trajectory record
# │          read the same values.
# │ Show:    25 ms setpoint period; 60 ms request delay vs. the 50 ms chunk
# │          renewal period; 575 ms motion-and-stop window (the 275 ms
# │          S-curve stop after 300 ms onset); 240 ms preferred admission;
# │          300 ms physical onset (60 ms slack); 278 ms latest admission;
# │          400 ms nominal end (H = 16 setpoints).
# │ How:     RM chunk step and horizon; the rest are scenario assumptions;
# │          eq-plan-action-chunk-horizon.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_frequency, fmt_latency, fmt_int

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class PlanningArmTimeline:
    """Replacement and stop timeline for the conveyor-tracking arm."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    t_period = RM.chunk_step  # category: chosen; chunk setpoint period, registry
    n_horizon = RM.chunk_horizon  # category: chosen; setpoints per chunk, registry
    t_chunk = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative; P99 chunk pass incl. vision, registry
    t_request = 60 * millisecond  # category: chosen; request delay
    f_renew = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen; chunk renewal rate, registry
    q_latency = 160 * millisecond  # category: chosen; design-tail replacement-latency target
    t_reserve = 20 * millisecond  # category: chosen; admission reserve
    t_stop = PlanningLeaseRule.t_arm_stop  # category: derived; arm S-curve stop duration, calc-planning-lease-rule
    t_blend = PlanningLeaseRule.t_blend  # category: chosen; blend deadline, calc-planning-lease-rule
    t_commit = PlanningLeaseRule.t_commit  # category: chosen; physical suffix onset, calc-planning-lease-rule

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    f_step = (1 / t_period).to("hertz")
    t_renew = (1 / f_renew).to(millisecond)
    request_slack = t_request - t_renew
    t_plan_exp = (n_horizon * t_period).to(millisecond)
    t_replace_min = t_request + q_latency + t_reserve
    commit_slack = t_commit - t_replace_min
    t_stop_end = t_commit + t_stop
    n_window = (t_stop_end / t_period).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(t_period.to(millisecond).magnitude - 25.0) < 1e-9, "chunk setpoint period changed")
    check(n_horizon == 16, "chunk horizon changed")
    check(abs(t_plan_exp.magnitude - 400.0) < 1e-9, "nominal end changed")
    check(q_latency > PlanningReplacementLedger.t_sum > t_chunk, "design-tail target no longer beyond the stage ledger")
    check(abs(t_replace_min.to(millisecond).magnitude - 240.0) < 1e-9, "replacement deadline changed")
    check(abs(commit_slack.to(millisecond).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "commitment slack changed")
    check(abs(t_stop_end.to(millisecond).magnitude - 575.0) < 1e-9, "arm stop end changed")
    check(abs(n_window - 23.0) < 1e-9, "authority-window duration equivalents changed")
    check(t_replace_min <= t_blend < t_commit < t_plan_exp < t_stop_end, "arm deadline order broken")
    check(abs(t_renew.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "chunk renewal period changed")
    check(request_slack.magnitude > 0, "request delay no longer exceeds the renewal period")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    t_period_str = fmt_latency(t_period, unit=millisecond)
    f_step_str = fmt_frequency(f_step)
    n_horizon_str = fmt_int(n_horizon)
    t_chunk_str = fmt_latency(t_chunk, unit=millisecond)
    t_request_str = fmt_latency(t_request, unit=millisecond)
    t_renew_str = fmt_latency(t_renew, unit=millisecond)
    request_slack_str = fmt_latency(request_slack, unit=millisecond)
    q_latency_str = fmt_latency(q_latency, unit=millisecond)
    t_reserve_str = fmt_latency(t_reserve, unit=millisecond)
    t_stop_str = fmt_latency(t_stop, unit=millisecond)
    t_replace_min_str = fmt_latency(t_replace_min, unit=millisecond)
    t_blend_str = fmt_latency(t_blend, unit=millisecond)
    t_commit_str = fmt_latency(t_commit, unit=millisecond)
    commit_slack_str = fmt_latency(commit_slack, unit=millisecond)
    t_plan_exp_str = fmt_latency(t_plan_exp, unit=millisecond)
    t_stop_end_str = fmt_latency(t_stop_end, unit=millisecond)
    n_window_str = fmt_int(n_window)
```

The machine's chunk policy emits a setpoint every `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_period_str`, `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.n_horizon_str` to a chunk, giving `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_plan_exp_str` of predicted nominal motion. In the running configuration, a replacement normally supersedes it after `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_renew_str`; loss of admission renewal expires the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str` lease. The unused prediction remains a candidate continuation, not additional tracking authority.

For comparison, consider an **alternate longer-lease schedule** on the same arm. A request delay of `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_request_str`, replacement target of `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.q_latency_str`, and scheduling reserve of `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_reserve_str` place preferred admission at `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_replace_min_str`. Physical stop onset is `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_commit_str`, leaving `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.commit_slack_str` between that target and onset. That interval separately covers the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_dispatch_str` decision-to-onset allowance, so admission must close by `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_alt_admission_cutoff_str` measured from this alternate schedule's origin, not from the last chunk admission. The reserve in @eq-plan-action-chunk-horizon includes both scheduling and physical-response allowances; the illustrated scheduling reserve alone is not the entire reserve. The separately checked stop lasts `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_stop_str`, set by the arm's deceleration and jerk bounds (@sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix), and completes at `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_stop_end_str`. These are stipulated or derived design values, not qualified timing measurements.

The alternate schedule explains how a complete record spans nominal motion and its stop; it is not the warehouse machine's operating renewal schedule. Its complete window spans `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.n_window_str` setpoint periods of duration, not that many stored samples: the stop is stored as a separately validated profile (its limits and phase durations), not as setpoints. The running machine would enter fallback well before this alternate admission target after a proposer stall. @Fig-11-seam-timeline-fallback places the two schedules on one time axis, each measured from its own origin and charged against its own clearance epoch.

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-timeline-figure
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SYNC GUARD FOR THE HAND-DRAWN TWO-SCHEDULE TIMELINE FIGURE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-11-seam-timeline-fallback (SVG labels are hand-typed).
# │
# │ Goal:    Fail the build if a cell value the figure draws changes.
# │ Show:    running 50 / 60 / 82 / 357 ms, 82 + 137.5 = 219.5 mm, 80.5 mm;
# │          alternate 240 / 278 / 300 / 400 / 575 ms, 60 + 137.5 = 197.5 mm,
# │          102.5 mm; 300 mm clearance.
# │ How:     Reads PlanningLeaseRule and PlanningArmTimeline; the alternate
# │          cruise is recomputed because PlanningC2Stop is defined later.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg, millisecond
from mlsysim.fmt import check

class PlanningTimelineFigure:
    """Values drawn in fig11_seam_timeline_fallback.svg."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    LR = PlanningLeaseRule  # category: derived; calc-planning-lease-rule
    AT = PlanningArmTimeline  # category: derived; calc-planning-arm-timeline

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    t_run_stop_end = (LR.t_lease_path + LR.t_arm_stop).to(millisecond)
    alt_cruise = (LR.v_arm * (AT.t_commit - AT.t_blend)).to(ureg.millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    def _ms(q):
        return q.to(millisecond).magnitude

    for _v, _drawn in (
        (LR.t_renew, 50),
        (LR.t_lease, 60),
        (LR.t_lease_path, 82),
        (t_run_stop_end, 357),
        (AT.t_replace_min, 240),
        (LR.t_alt_admission_cutoff, 278),
        (AT.t_commit, 300),
        (AT.t_plan_exp, 400),
        (AT.t_stop_end, 575),
    ):
        check(abs(_ms(_v) - _drawn) < 1e-9, f"timeline figure label {_drawn} ms is stale")
    check(abs(LR.arm_stop_dist.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude - 137.5) < 1e-9, "figure stop distance is stale")
    check(abs(LR.lease_total.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude - 219.5) < 1e-9, "figure running travel is stale")
    check(abs(LR.lease_margin.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude - 80.5) < 1e-9, "figure running margin is stale")
    check(abs(alt_cruise.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "figure alternate cruise is stale")
    check(abs(LR.commit_margin.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude - 102.5) < 1e-9, "figure alternate margin is stale")
    check(abs(LR.d_arm_clear.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude - 300.0) < 1e-9, "figure clearance is stale")
```

::: {#fig-11-seam-timeline-fallback fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Two lease schedules for the arm**: On the running lease (top), a stalled proposer lapses the lease 60 ms after the last admission, and the tick, bus, and onset allowance (amber) delays the resident stop to 82 ms. On the alternate schedule (bottom), admission must close by 278 ms so the matched stop begins at the 300 ms commitment; the unused nominal setpoints run to 400 ms. Each margin is charged against its own clearance check and still excludes sensing and model reserves." fig-alt="Two horizontal timelines on a shared axis from 0 to 600 milliseconds. Top: tracking until the lease lapses at 60 ms, a response interval to stop onset at 82 ms, and an S-curve stop at rest by 357 ms, using 219.5 of 300 millimeters of clearance. Bottom: tracking until commitment at 300 ms with preferred admission at 240 and cutoff at 278, nominal end at 400, and a matched stop at rest by 575 ms, using 197.5 of 300 millimeters."}
![](images/svg/fig11_seam_timeline_fallback.svg){width="100%"}
:::

Sustaining the running renewal cadence also requires a throughput argument. The illustrative `{python} PlanningReplacementLedger.t_sum_str` replacement latency exceeds the `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_renew_str` renewal period. Overlapped requests can meet that cadence only if the allocated stages have sufficient capacity and bounded contention; overlap cannot be inferred from the latency sum alone. Until loaded testing supports the schedule, the stop remains the specified response to missed renewal.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_replacement_latency_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal time bars on one millisecond axis: capture to dispatch at 51.6 and capture to admission at 114.9, both extending past a vertical line for the 50 millisecond renewal period and a second line for the 60 millisecond lease."}

*A `{python} PlanningReplacementLedger.t_sum_str` replacement path outlasts the `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_renew_str` renewal, so requests must overlap.*
:::

Both schedules remain bounded by target-evidence age. Even under a qualified local tracker, @sec-intent-goals-expire finds that one mug observation cannot justify the full alternate commitment window. The constructive route is a staged approach: follow a checked prefix through a qualified clear corridor, acquire a closer wrist observation, and renew tracked target segments from fresh captures. The terminal grasp is admitted only when its full profile fits the current target tolerance and validity window. The overall reach may outlast one observation; each executed segment must still have current support. A newer proposal header cannot renew old evidence, and loss of that support ends TRACK through the state-matched fallback.

The physical Push-T recoveries that @chi2024diffusionpolicy report show what replanning can accomplish when new observations arrive. An articulated pusher moves a T-shaped block toward a target using a diffusion policy that predicts $T_p = 16$ steps and executes $T_a = 6$ before replanning. The examples show recovery after camera occlusion, displacement during an approach, and displacement near completion [@chi2024diffusionpolicy]. They demonstrate correction of a task trajectory, not checked derivative continuity or stopping behavior during inference starvation. A production admission decision still needs an independently executable stop within the available clearance.

### Future-state conditioning and execution delay compensation {#sec-planning-future-state-conditioning}

Because neural trajectory synthesis requires nonzero wall-clock compute time, a replacement plan cannot be initiated from the robot's physical state measured at the moment inference is triggered. Initiating planning from a stale measurement creates the **Stale-State Paradox**. When the sequence model finishes, the new trajectory begins where the arm was when inference started, so following it would command the mechanism to jump back across the distance it traveled during the computation, a step discontinuity in position, velocity, and acceleration.

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-stale-pose-gap
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STALE REQUEST-EPOCH POSE GAP
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-goal-to-trajectory (projected-seam paragraph).
# │
# │ Goal:    Show how far a moving reference runs ahead of a pose captured when
# │          the replacement was requested.
# │ Show:    0.50 rad/s x 80 ms = 0.040 rad (2.29 degrees); up to 28 mm of
# │          tool motion at the 0.70 m planar reach.
# │ How:     Illustrative delay and joint speed; reach from
# │          calc-planning-two-link-arm (lever arm bounded by the reach).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg, millisecond, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_angular_velocity, fmt_angle, fmt_latency, fmt_length

class PlanningStalePoseGap:
    """Reference lag of a stale request-epoch pose."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    t_delay = 80 * millisecond  # category: illustrative; replacement delay
    w_joint = 0.50 * ureg.radian / second  # category: illustrative; constant joint speed

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    gap = (w_joint * t_delay).to(ureg.radian)
    gap_deg = gap.to(ureg.degree)
```
