### Mobile-base planning under nonholonomic constraints {#sec-planning-mobile-base}

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-mobile-base
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ DYNAMIC WINDOW AND CLASSICAL ADMISSIBILITY FOR THE BASE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-mobile-base.
# │
# │ Goal:    Size the base's dynamic window over one chunk renewal, and show
# │          what the classical admissibility test admits on the rack-end arc.
# │ Show:    2.0 m/s^2 x 50 ms = +/-0.1 m/s; sqrt(2 x 1.10 m x 2.0 m/s^2) =
# │          2.10 m/s, above the 1.5 m/s drive limit.
# │ How:     RM base acceleration and velocity limits and chunk renewal
# │          (registry); AISLE rack-end clear distance and a_brake; DWA
# │          admissibility v <= sqrt(2 dist a_b) (fox1997dynamic, eq. 14).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg, millisecond
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration, fmt_latency, fmt_length

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class PlanningMobileBase:
    """Dynamic-window width over one renewal and the classical admissible speed."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    a_base = RM.base.max_acceleration  # category: illustrative; base acceleration limit, registry
    v_drive = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative; drive limit, registry
    f_renew = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen; chunk renewal rate, registry
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative; credible deceleration, registry
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative; rack-end clear distance, registry

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    t_renew = (1 / f_renew).to(millisecond)
    dv_window = (a_base * t_renew).to(ureg.meter / ureg.second)
    v_admissible = ((2 * d_clear * a_brake) ** 0.5).to(ureg.meter / ureg.second)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(dv_window.magnitude - 0.1) < 1e-12, "dynamic window width changed")
    check(abs(v_admissible.magnitude - 2.0976) < 1e-4, "classical admissible speed changed")
    check(v_admissible > v_drive, "classical test no longer admits the drive limit")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    a_base_str = fmt_acceleration(a_base)
    t_renew_str = fmt_latency(t_renew, unit=millisecond)
    dv_window_str = fmt_velocity(dv_window, precision=1)
    v_admissible_str = fmt_velocity(v_admissible, precision=2)
    v_drive_str = fmt_velocity(v_drive)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=ureg.meter, precision=2)
```

The base proposes motion under a constraint the arm does not have. Its two driven wheels roll without slipping sideways, so the base cannot translate along its axle. With heading $\theta$, forward speed $v$, and turn rate $\omega$, the differential-drive (unicycle) model is

$$\dot x = v\cos\theta, \qquad \dot y = v\sin\theta, \qquad \dot\theta = \omega, \qquad \dot x\sin\theta - \dot y\cos\theta = 0$$ {#eq-plan-unicycle}

The last relation in @eq-plan-unicycle is a **nonholonomic constraint**\index{Nonholonomic constraint!differential drive},[^fn-holonomic-hertz-etymology] one that restricts velocity without restricting reachable position [@siciliano2009robotics]. The base can reach any pose in the aisle, but a sideways offset costs a maneuver of turning, driving, and turning back, so its planner searches over feasible motions rather than straight configuration-space steps (@fig-11-nonholonomic-base). Each wheel's speed is $v \pm \omega b/2$ for track width $b$, so each wheel's drive limit bounds a combination of forward and turning speed.

[^fn-holonomic-hertz-etymology]: **Holonomic** (Greek *holos*, whole, and *nomos*, law): @hertz1894prinzipien introduced the term for systems whose constraints obey integral laws, relations among positions alone, in contrast to material systems in general, which obey only differential laws. A wheel's no-slip rule is a differential law that cannot be integrated into such a relation. The distinction decides the planner's search space, since a holonomic arm can be planned as a path through configuration space while the base must be planned through its controls.\index{Holonomic constraint!etymology}

::: {#fig-11-nonholonomic-base fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**What the wheels allow**: (a) A differential-drive base with track width $b$ can move forward at $v$ and turn at $\omega$ about the center of its axle, but its wheels cannot roll sideways. (b) A pure sideways offset is still reachable, as a maneuver rather than a step: turn in place, drive, and turn back. Proportions are schematic." fig-alt="Two top-view panels of a rectangular base with a drive wheel on each side. In the left panel, a solid arrow points forward along the heading, a curved arrow shows turning, a bracket marks the track width, and a dashed arrow pointing sideways is crossed out. In the right panel, a dashed sideways arrow between a start and a goal pose is crossed out, and a second path shows the base turned a quarter turn in place at the start, driving straight to the goal, and turning back, with the three steps numbered."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-planning-nonholonomic-base
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ NONHOLONOMIC BASE (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-11-nonholonomic-base in @sec-planning-mobile-base.
# │
# │ Goal:    Make the rolling constraint of @eq-plan-unicycle physical: the base
# │          has two velocity inputs and cannot translate along its axle.
# │ Show:    admissible v and omega, the forbidden sideways velocity, and the
# │          turn-drive-turn maneuver that reaches a sideways offset.
# │ How:     Schematic geometry; no physical values are drawn.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import viz
import numpy as np
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyArrowPatch, Polygon
from matplotlib.transforms import Affine2D

R = viz.VOL4_ROLES
viz.set_book_style()
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def _footprint(ax, x, y, th, ghost=False):
    """Base outline, drive wheels on the axle, and heading tick (schematic proportions)."""
    L, W, wl, ww = 0.9, 0.6, 0.26, 0.09
    tr = Affine2D().rotate(th).translate(x, y) + ax.transData
    ec = R["neutral"] if ghost else R["structural"]
    ax.add_patch(
        Rectangle((-L / 2, -W / 2), L, W, fc="none" if ghost else "#EEF3F1", ec=ec, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)) if ghost else "-", transform=tr, zorder=3)
    )
    if not ghost:
        for s in (1, -1):
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((-wl / 2, s * W / 2 - ww / 2), wl, ww, fc=R["structural"], ec="none", transform=tr, zorder=4))
    ax.add_patch(Polygon([[L / 2 - 0.16, 0.1], [L / 2 - 0.02, 0], [L / 2 - 0.16, -0.1]], closed=True, fc=ec, ec="none", transform=tr, zorder=4))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.8))
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.axis("off")
_footprint(ax, 0, 0, 0)
# allowed: forward speed along the heading, turn rate about the axle center
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((0.5, 0), (1.25, 0), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=11, color=R["structural"], lw=1.4, zorder=5))
ax.text(1.28, 0, r"$v$", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=10, color=R["structural"])
ax.add_patch(
    FancyArrowPatch(
        (0.28, -0.52), (-0.28, -0.52), connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.45", arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10, color=R["structural"], lw=1.1, zorder=5
    )
)
ax.text(0, -0.8, r"$\omega$", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=10, color=R["structural"])
# forbidden: translation along the axle
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((0, 0.33), (0, 0.95), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=11, color=R["neutral"], lw=1.2, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=5))
ax.plot([-0.09, 0.09], [0.55, 0.73], color=R["neutral"], lw=1.6, zorder=6)
ax.plot([-0.09, 0.09], [0.73, 0.55], color=R["neutral"], lw=1.6, zorder=6)
ax.text(0.14, 0.95, "no sideways velocity", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=R["neutral"])
ax.annotate("", xy=(-0.55, 0.3), xytext=(-0.55, -0.3), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=R["neutral"], lw=0.8))
ax.text(-0.6, 0, r"$b$", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=10, color=R["neutral"])
# a sideways offset: the direct step is inadmissible; turn in place, drive, turn back
x0, dy = 2.9, 1.7
_footprint(ax, x0, 0, 0)
_footprint(ax, x0, 0, np.pi / 2, ghost=True)
_footprint(ax, x0, dy, np.pi / 2, ghost=True)
_footprint(ax, x0, dy, 0)
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x0, 0.5), (x0, dy - 0.5), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=11, color=R["proposal"], lw=1.4, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=5))
for yy, lab in ((0, "1  turn in place"), (dy / 2, "2  drive"), (dy, "3  turn back")):
    ax.text(x0 + 0.62, yy, lab, ha="left", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=R["proposal"])
xs = x0 - 1.0
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs, 0), (xs, dy), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=11, color=R["neutral"], lw=1.2, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=5))
ax.plot([xs - 0.09, xs + 0.09], [dy / 2 - 0.09, dy / 2 + 0.09], color=R["neutral"], lw=1.6, zorder=6)
ax.plot([xs - 0.09, xs + 0.09], [dy / 2 + 0.09, dy / 2 - 0.09], color=R["neutral"], lw=1.6, zorder=6)
ax.text(xs - 0.14, dy / 2, "direct\nsideways\nstep", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=R["neutral"])
ax.text(0, 2.2, "(a) admissible velocities", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=R["neutral"])
ax.text(x0, 2.2, "(b) a sideways offset", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=R["neutral"])
ax.set_xlim(-0.9, 4.6)
ax.set_ylim(-0.95, 2.45)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

Local planners enforce these limits by planning in velocity space over a short horizon. The dynamic window approach [@fox1997dynamic] treats each pair $(v,\omega)$ as a circular arc and keeps only two kinds. Reachable pairs lie within the next interval's acceleration limits; with the base's `{python} PlanningMobileBase.a_base_str` limit and the `{python} PlanningMobileBase.t_renew_str` chunk renewal, that window spans `{python} PlanningMobileBase.dv_window_str` either side of the current forward speed. Admissible pairs are those from which the base can stop before the nearest obstacle on the arc, $v \le \sqrt{2\,d_{\text{arc}}(v,\omega)\,a_{\text{brake}}}$. Among the survivors, the planner maximizes a weighted score of heading toward the goal, clearance, and speed. Model predictive path integral control (MPPI) [@williams2017information] replaces that grid with many randomly perturbed control sequences rolled forward through the model and weighted by cost, and the ROS 2 navigation stack ships both families [@macenski2023desks].

The admissibility test is this chapter's stopping condition applied to every candidate arc, but its classical form charges only constant-deceleration braking. On a straight arc to the `{python} PlanningMobileBase.d_clear_str` rack-end clear distance it admits speeds up to `{python} PlanningMobileBase.v_admissible_str`, above the `{python} PlanningMobileBase.v_drive_str` drive limit, while the budget of @sec-planning-base-stopping-budget, which adds reaction delay, localization and margin terms, and the jerk-limited stop, already fails at the drive limit. A base proposer, whether a local planner or the chunk policy's base velocity targets, therefore supplies candidates; the permission path applies the complete stopping budget to each, and @sec-enforcement derives the speed at which that budget holds.

The generator choice changes how a candidate is found and how much admission work it creates. It does not change the response to an invalid candidate or a changed world. Those failures must be distinguished because rejecting a replacement need not invalidate the motion already under way.

## Trajectory Planning Failure Modes and Infeasible Seams {#sec-planning-failure-modes}

A replacement for the mug reach can fail in the candidate itself, at its join to the moving arm, or after admission when the world changes. Where the failure first becomes visible determines which subsystem has the evidence to reject the motion and how much time remains to stop. Candidate and boundary checks address the first two cases; runtime monitoring addresses the third.

### Pre-execution limit and boundary checkers {#sec-planning-pre-execution-checkers}

Before any proposed trajectory setpoint can influence actuator registers, the deterministic safety MCU screens the candidate record through two independent admission gates within a measured worst-case time budget. Fixed-degree seam calculations have bounded work per axis; checking a complete setpoint sequence also depends on its length:

1.  **Pre-execution Bound Checker:** Evaluates the proposed neural action chunk in isolation against intrinsic kinematic, dynamic, and stopping invariants across the full candidate horizon $[t_{\mathrm{start}}, t_{\mathrm{plan\_exp}}]$. Beyond testing margin functions $M(t) = L_{\mathrm{limit}} - |x(t)|$ across joint positions $q(t)$, contracted velocity limits $|\dot{q}(t)| \le v_{\max} - \frac{1}{2} a_{\max} T_s$ (@eq-plan-contracted-velocity-limit, or the $\frac{1}{4}$ reserve under a stated jerk bound), and free-space inverse-dynamics joint torques, sampled with a bound on their variation between samples, $|\boldsymbol{\tau}(t)| = |\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})\dot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{q})| \le \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{rated}}$, the checker enforces the crucial stopping invariant: the candidate's matched stopping suffix must satisfy $d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clear}}$ within observed free space. Any knot or interior interval where $M(t) < 0$ or where stopping runway breaches clearance triggers immediate rejection, logging a diagnostic fault record naming the joint index, timestamp, and negative margin. Rejection at the admission gate causes no mechanical shudder or physical pause: the tracking controller can continue the previously admitted trajectory only while its own state, evidence, lease, and stopping reserve remain valid. A rejected replacement does not renew that lease.
2.  **Boundary Checker:** Evaluates the transition seam between the currently executing trajectory $A$ and the candidate replacement $B$ at $t_{\mathrm{seam}}$. Because unconstrained sequence decoders predict open-loop action tokens without terminal derivative matching, concatenating raw chunks can leave acceleration steps. At earlier admission it checks the reachable seam-state envelope; at activation, the boundary checker uses encoder-based estimates $(\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{meas}}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}_{\mathrm{meas}}, \ddot{\mathbf{q}}_{\mathrm{meas}})$ and their error bounds, estimates the physical seam gap $(\Delta\mathbf{q}, \Delta\dot{\mathbf{q}}, \Delta\ddot{\mathbf{q}})$, and evaluates whether an analytical $C^2$ quintic bridge (@eq-plan-quintic-spline-matrix) can reconcile the boundary while meeting torque limits and the drive's voltage and current-slew constraints. The one-tick estimate $\tau_{\mathrm{request}} = J_{\mathrm{eff}} \frac{\Delta\dot q}{T_c}$ screens a velocity mismatch; the finite bridge still needs its own interior checks.

For the CSG-25-50 joint of the seam notebook, counting only its `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.j_reflected_str` reflected rotor inertia over one `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.dt_tick_str` tick and allocating the whole `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_peak_rated_str` repeated-peak rating to this acceleration gives an *idealized ceiling* of `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.dq_ceiling_str` on $\Delta\dot q$. Available margin is smaller after link and payload inertia, gravity, friction, other commanded torque, current rise time, and thermal or bus limits are accounted for. The permission path must use that state-dependent margin and the measured drive response when evaluating a finite bridge. It rejects a direct velocity discontinuity even if its one-tick arithmetic falls below that ceiling; a bounded $C^2$ bridge and its interior checks are still required.[^fn-inc-seam-trip]

[^fn-inc-seam-trip]: **Drive and resonance response**\index{Drivetrain!resonant frequency}\index{Inverter!desaturation trip}: A sharp command can excite a joint's *identified* flexible modes, but their frequencies and damping depend on the transmission and load. Current limiting, desaturation detection, DC-bus response, and shutdown depend on the selected driver and its configuration; one vendor's desaturation-protection design note shows how such trip thresholds are set [@chen2025tpsi3133].

### Runtime tracking monitors and unmodeled contact trips {#sec-planning-runtime-monitors}

After admission, a slipping payload or new contact can invalidate the dynamics used to check the plan. Runtime monitoring must detect that change while the remaining clearance still supports a response.

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-monitor-trip
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RUNTIME MONITOR TRIP THRESHOLDS FOR THE ARM
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-failure-modes (runtime monitors paragraph).
# │
# │ Goal:    Derive the tool-position error trip from the budgeted clearance and
# │          the deflection allowance, beside the unmodeled-contact threshold.
# │ Show:    0.020 m - 0.005 m = 0.015 m; 10 N contact threshold.
# │ How:     Illustrative clearance, allowance, and contact threshold.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_length, fmt_force

class PlanningMonitorTrip:
    """Position-error trip threshold and contact threshold for the arm."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    d_clearance = 0.020 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative; budgeted clearance past the conveyor guard
    d_deflect = 0.005 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative; payload deflection and gearbox compliance
    f_contact = 10 * ureg.newton  # category: illustrative; unmodeled free-space contact threshold

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    eps_pos = (d_clearance - d_deflect).to(ureg.meter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(eps_pos.magnitude - 0.015) < 1e-12, "position error trip changed")
    check(eps_pos.magnitude > 0, "deflection allowance consumes the clearance")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    d_clearance_str = fmt_length(d_clearance, unit=ureg.meter, precision=3)
    d_deflect_str = fmt_length(d_deflect, unit=ureg.meter, precision=3)
    eps_pos_str = fmt_length(eps_pos, unit=ureg.meter, precision=3)
    f_contact_str = fmt_force(f_contact, precision=0)
```

Independent **runtime monitors**\index{Runtime monitor} detect changed-world infeasibility by observing four dedicated signals, comprising joint state divergence, tracking error velocity, unexpected contact wrenches, and the invalidation of the geometric assumptions the record declares (@sec-planning-trajectory-contract). This derivation demonstrates **Spatial Margin Budgeting**: geometric obstacle clearance cannot be allocated entirely to tracking error. Physical compliance and mechanical deflection under load consume clearance before any tracking divergence occurs. The tracking error allowance $\epsilon_{\mathrm{pos}}$ is therefore the total swept-volume clearance less the structural deflection and gearbox compliance allowance $\delta_{\mathrm{deflect}}$. For the mobile manipulator's arm reaching past the conveyor guard, a budgeted swept-volume clearance of `{python} PlanningMonitorTrip.d_clearance_str` and an unmodeled payload deflection and gearbox compliance allowance $\delta_{\mathrm{deflect}}$ of `{python} PlanningMonitorTrip.d_deflect_str` leave an allowance $\epsilon_{\mathrm{pos}}$ of `{python} PlanningMonitorTrip.eps_pos_str`. This remainder is an upper allocation before post-trip growth and uncertainty reserve, not a usable trip threshold by itself. Detection, dispatch, and actuator-onset travel, the fallback swept motion, and state-estimation uncertainty require separate reserved clearance. The allowance caps the tracking bound rather than replacing it. The arm tracker's own validated bound, the arm's instance of the $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$ that @sec-enforcement-handoff validates for the base, must sit inside those `{python} PlanningMonitorTrip.eps_pos_str`, and the per-tick check trips on $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$. If measured Cartesian tool-position error $\|\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{tool,actual}}(t)-\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{tool,planned}}(t)\|$ exceeds $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$, or a six-axis force-torque sensor reports an unmodeled `{python} PlanningMonitorTrip.f_contact_str` contact in this free-space example, the monitor revokes nominal tracking and requests the validated state-matched fallback. Actual deceleration begins after the measured detection, dispatch, and actuator response delays.

A plan can also exhaust its nominal references before the next candidate passes admission. The MCU must not wait for the execution pointer to run off the array or treat a final-position hold as a stop. On this machine the chunk lease ends the wait first, and the alternate schedule separately enforces the pre-onset admission cutoff of @sec-planning-behavior-seam, which the MCU applies in its own monotonic clock. Complete stopping clearance includes detection, dispatch, actuator response, and motion under the selected profile; an assumed constant deceleration is insufficient for the $C^2$ worked suffix.

Every detector in this section relies on an explicit contract between the trajectory generator and the execution runtime. A plan delivered as a raw list of coordinates, without its valid lifespan, clearance bounds, boundary derivatives, and fallback, leaves the permission path unable to tell whether an ongoing motion remains safe or has drifted into infeasibility.

## The Trajectory Record {#sec-planning-trajectory-contract}

Each time the chunk policy proposes `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.n_horizon_str` new setpoints for the reach toward the mug, the permission path must decide whether to admit them without asking the planner anything. The trajectory record\index{Trajectory record!contract}\index{Cyber-physical contract!trajectory planning}, immutable and handed over at every replanning cycle, makes that decision possible. The record is less a message format than a **Cyber-Physical Contract**, in which each field states a physical invariant the permission path can check across the causal boundary.

The record lets the MCU decide without continuing cooperation from the proposer, through the staged admission check and latched stop of @sec-planning-inevitable-collision-states. A host crash cannot remove that resident stop, although executing it still requires sensing, drive energy, and braking authority. The inputs established at the planning handoff remain part of the record's lineage: scene memory supplies geometry and clearance, and intent supplies the target, tolerances, effort ceilings, and parent lease. The completed record passes those assumptions with the motion to @sec-enforcement, where current state determines per-tick permission.

Each field records a reason the motion was admitted. Boundary derivatives establish what the seam must join; deadlines state when nominal motion must yield to stopping; the sidecar identifies the scene and load assumptions under which the checks held. The record preserves those obligations for the execution runtime rather than turning the planner's claimed feasibility into permission.

The trajectory record answers to the intent lease of @sec-intent-lease, whose digest it carries as its parent, and every setpoint it proposes pursues the lease's target without exceeding its effort ceilings. The record stores the motion as setpoint arrays or spline coefficients, together with the sample cadence (on this machine a `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_period_str` period $\Delta t_{\text{step}}$, a `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.f_step_str` setpoint stream), the nominal end $t_{\mathrm{plan\_exp}}$ (`{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_plan_exp_str` for one chunk), and SI units. With the frame and evidence time of @sec-planning-handoff, the units, and the cadence in the handoff, the joint controller interpolates setpoints and evaluates derivatives without frame mismatches or reliance on ambient system clocks.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Trajectory feasibility proposals are separately checked against conditional control barrier functions in @sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission.
:::

Physical feasibility depends on the scene and load used to validate the plan. The immutable sidecar therefore identifies obstacle-map epochs, payload and friction assumptions, limits, validator version, measured margin, and the source observation, and a digest in the fixed header binds it to the setpoints. The validator proves the stop feasible only under these assumptions, and they may claim no more than evaluation sampled, so the payload and friction the sidecar declares must lie inside the target Operational Design Domain (ODD) of @sec-evaluation-logs. The permission path revokes TRACK when live state leaves them, since a recorded margin holds only for the scene it was computed against. Solver seed and model hash belong in the audit sidecar for reproducibility where the toolchain supports it, not in the servo's per-tick path.

On this machine the chunk policy's output supplies only the nominal part of each trajectory record. Planning adds the seam state, the four deadlines, and the matched stop suffix, so the permission path admits one stream of records. The fixed header groups each record's fields by purpose. Lineage fields give a sequence number, the evidence time $t_0$, and the digest of the parent intent lease. Timing fields give the four deadlines of @sec-planning-handoff, and the record's tracking authority ends at the earliest of its pre-onset stop-dispatch cutoff, the lapse of the chunk lease (@sec-nervous-cadences) `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str` after the last admitted chunk, the parent intent's expiry, and target-evidence expiry. Seam fields give the frame, each joint's entry state $(q,\dot q,\ddot q)$, and the certified stop-suffix polynomial coefficients ($d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clear}}$). Content fields give the payload kind and size and one digest over the setpoint payload and the sidecar. A variable-length setpoint payload and immutable provenance/assumption sidecar are outside the fixed header, and the MCU verifies their digest before the admission check of @sec-planning-behavior-seam. The payload digest binds content, and the parent digest binds lineage. The record carries no keyed tag, because the permission path admits a proposal by its content rather than its origin (@sec-nervous-cadences).

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ **Byte layout:** The trajectory record's field offsets and sizes are given in @sec-appendix-systems-wire-trajectory.
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-record-trace
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FILLED TRAJECTORY RECORD FOR THE REACH TOWARD THE MUG
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-trajectory-contract (filled record paragraph).
# │
# │ Goal:    Gather the worked record's field values from the cells that own
# │          them and add the one sidecar value no earlier cell holds.
# │ Show:    3 kg payload bound; 16 x 25 ms = 400 ms nominal end.
# │ How:     RM arm payload capacity; the other fields read
# │          PlanningLeaseRule, PlanningArmTimeline, and PlanningC2Stop.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import kilogram
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_mass

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class PlanningRecordTrace:
    """Sidecar payload bound for the worked trajectory record."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    m_payload = RM.arm.payload_capacity  # category: datasheet; arm payload capacity, registry

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    t_nominal = (PlanningArmTimeline.n_horizon * PlanningArmTimeline.t_period).to(PlanningArmTimeline.t_plan_exp.units)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(m_payload.to(kilogram).magnitude - 3.0) < 1e-9, "arm payload capacity changed")
    check(t_nominal == PlanningArmTimeline.t_plan_exp, "nominal end disagrees with horizon x period")
    check(PlanningLeaseRule.lease_total <= PlanningLeaseRule.d_arm_clear, "lease-path stop no longer inside the clearance")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    m_payload_str = fmt_mass(m_payload, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
```

Filled in for the mug reach, the running record retains the illustrative geometric endpoints of the longer-lease comparison but is superseded or stopped under the shorter operating lease. Its parent is the mug's intent lease, bound by digest; its frame is the machine's base frame, and every time field is in the MCU monotonic clock. Measured from $t_{\mathrm{start}}$, the timing fields hold the `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_commit_str` commitment, the `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_plan_exp_str` nominal end that `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.n_horizon_str` setpoints at `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_period_str` give, and the `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_stop_end_str` stop end; the `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_blend_str` blend target belongs to the alternate schedule, not the operating renewal cadence or the fixed header. The seam fields hold a `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_arm_stop_str` jerk-limited $C^2$ suffix, bounded by `{python} PlanningC2Stop.a_arm_peak_str` and `{python} PlanningC2Stop.j_arm_str`, that brings the arm to rest from its `{python} PlanningC2Stop.v_arm_str` TCP limit in `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_stop_dist_str`. While the record is in force, the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str` chunk lease bounds its tracking, a lapse leads to the state-matched fallback along a path that uses `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.lease_total_str` of the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.d_arm_clear_str` clearance. The separate `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_alt_admission_cutoff_str` cutoff belongs to the alternate schedule's origin and later clearance check; it grants no extension of the running lease. The sidecar declares a payload of at most `{python} PlanningRecordTrace.m_payload_str`, free space until the grasp, and a scene inside the target ODD. Each field is one the permission path checks at admission or monitors on every tick, without asking the planner what it meant.

In the worked case the deadlines satisfy $t_{\mathrm{start}}\le t_{\mathrm{commit}}<t_{\mathrm{plan\_exp}}<t_{\mathrm{stop\_end}}$. The MCU applies these deadlines under the TRACK and STOP rules of @sec-planning-handoff, and a header timestamp cannot make a mismatched suffix safe. A log records evidence, request, validation, admission, activation, transfer, and stop-completion times in a common converted domain so actual response delay can be measured.

Every record in the runtime chain, from the observation contract through the belief record and the intent lease to the trajectory record itself, now names what it rests on and when it expires. The trajectory record proves only what the planner could foresee, a stop feasible from the states reachable before commitment under the scene and load in its sidecar. Several of the fallacies that follow mistake that bounded proof for a broader one.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-planning-fallacies-pitfalls}

A trajectory remains feasible only while its physical assumptions hold at chunk boundaries and during fallback. Admission and execution checks must address those transitions as well as the nominal path.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Static admission checks protect a machine against obstacle displacements during active execution.*

**Static geometry is an admission precondition, not an execution certificate; dynamic reality always requires runtime monitoring.** The arm begins an admitted reach toward the mug with the conveyor guard clear of its swept volume. During execution, a coworker slides a tote into the tool's path. The admission check was correct for the earlier geometry but no longer supports continued motion. Execution monitoring\index{Execution monitoring!collision detection} must detect the changed clearance and begin deceleration while sufficient stopping room remains. The design must bound how quickly workspace changes become visible via sensor bus latency\index{Network!bus latency} and reserve the stopping margin needed to respond before the updated geometry becomes impossible to avoid.

**Architect's countermeasure**: Couple host spatial screening to bounded, qualified local clearance evidence consumed by the MCU; allocate its refresh latency and memory explicitly. If an unmodeled obstacle breaches the reserved spatial margin $\delta_{\text{pos}}$, immediately abort nominal tracking and initiate the validated state-matched fallback.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Checking each action chunk alone without examining the motion the chunks compose.*

**Individual chunk feasibility does not imply composed trajectory stability; stochastic neural chatter can overstress a transmission.** When sequence models (such as diffusion policies or transformers) are sampled stochastically, successive chunks can exhibit high-frequency directional reversals or boundary acceleration mismatches. While every individual chunk satisfies kinematic position and velocity bounds, their concatenation produces rapid torque reversals $\Delta\tau = J_{\text{eff}} \Delta\ddot{q}$. Amplified by reflected rotor inertia ($N_g^2 J_{\text{rotor}}$), this chatter can excite identified flexible modes, increase transmission wear, and add Joule heating ($I^2R$)\index{Motor!Joule heating} in stator windings. Admission must evaluate derivative continuity across each seam, enforce $C^2$ quintic smoothing, and retain motion history to reject oscillating chunk sequences before they excite mechanical modes.

**Architect's countermeasure**: Enforce multi-chunk frequency and reversal monitoring across the execution window. Reject sequences whose spectrum or repeated effort exceeds the identified mechanical or thermal envelope. If filtering changes a candidate, repeat the full trajectory, seam, and stop checks before admission.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Delaying fallback transition past the hard stopping horizon in the hope that delayed compute finishes.*

**An overdue compute cycle never justifies extending a physical commitment deadline. Hope is not a deceleration profile.** In the alternate schedule with its `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_alt_admission_cutoff_str` admission cutoff, the worked arm's record ends its nominal setpoints at `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_plan_exp_str` and carries a `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_stop_str` matched stop suffix that must finish by `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_stop_end_str`, so the MCU must dispatch fallback\index{Fallback trajectory!commitment point} by `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_alt_admission_cutoff_str` to achieve physical onset at `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_commit_str` unless it has admitted a valid replacement. At that point the application processor reports inference nearly complete, but it has not delivered an executable plan. Waiting spends the runway reserved for deceleration. The MCU must follow the matched stop suffix at the commitment point. Progress reports cannot extend a mechanical stopping budget; only a newly validated trajectory can justify continued execution.

**Architect's countermeasure**: Bind the commitment deadline $t_{\mathrm{commit}}$ strictly to the MCU monotonic hardware timer. Close replacement admission and dispatch the resident stop early enough to meet physical onset at commitment, ignoring host progress updates.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Relying solely on feedforward dynamic models when physical contact or payload mass can change abruptly.*

**Feedforward model inversion without closed-loop disturbance bounds turns payload loss into explosive runaway.** The arm lifts an item near its `{python} PlanningRecordTrace.m_payload_str` payload bound using feedforward torque\index{Feedforward control!torque demand} computed for the loaded arm. The item slips from the gripper, but the drives keep applying the same lifting torque to the now unloaded arm, so it accelerates upward. The admitted trajectory has not changed; the dynamics that made its commands appropriate have. Feedback monitoring\index{Feedback control!error monitoring} must detect the resulting tracking error and constrain the commands within the available margin before a mechanical limit strike or thermal derating\index{Motor!thermal derating}. A feedforward model improves nominal tracking, but it cannot replace runtime checks for abrupt changes in payload or contact.

**Architect's countermeasure**: Implement real-time torque and tracking error monitoring ($\|\mathbf{x}_{\text{actual}} - \mathbf{x}_{\text{ref}}\| \le \epsilon_{\text{track}}$) at the `{python} PlanningOpeningMachine.f_track_str` servo layer. If sudden payload detachment or contact mismatch causes acceleration to spike, clamp motor currents and transition to compliance or emergency stop.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *A trajectory can omit an achievable terminal stopping suffix if replacement plans are expected to arrive in time.*

**A trajectory without a pre-latched stopping continuation is an unhedged bet on infinite compute availability.** At its `{python} PlanningC2Stop.v_drive_str` drive limit, the mobile manipulator's base needs `{python} PlanningC2Stop.s_drive_time_str` for even the shortest stop its bounds allow, the S-curve of $T=v_c/a_{\max}+a_{\max}/j_{\max}$ at the credible `{python} PlanningC2Stop.a_brake_str` and the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.j_base_str` jerk bound.\index{Trajectory!braking time} A proposed suffix sized by the constant-deceleration time $v_c/a_{\text{brake}}$, `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_const_drive_str`, cannot be met by any profile that ramps its deceleration, so it must exceed the deceleration bound, the jerk bound, or both, past what the loaded rack tolerates. Expecting the next plan to arrive does not make this fallback executable. The admission gate must check that the suffix respects $a_{\max}$ and $j_{\max}$ throughout, which the S-curve's closed form makes a check of $T_{\mathrm{stop}}$ against @eq-plan-c2-stopping-suffix, and certify $d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clear}}$, rejecting any record that fails. Every accepted trajectory needs a physically certified termination path\index{Fallback trajectory!achievability} for the inevitable occasion when an inference pass is delayed.

**Architect's countermeasure**: Require every candidate trajectory record to include a complete, closed-form $C^2$ stopping profile along its admitted path whose deceleration and jerk stay within the load's bounds and whose distance satisfies $d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clear}}$ within verified clearance. Reject any record at the admission gate that lacks this certified, independently executable return ticket.

:::

## Summary {#sec-planning-summary}

A trajectory turns a goal into timed motion, and on a moving machine it must settle three questions that a path alone leaves open: how long the motion remains executable, how it joins the motion already under way, and how the machine stops if no successor arrives. The mug reach can progress through renewed, checked prefixes without forcing the overall task into one observation window. Prediction provides candidate motion; fresh evidence, timely admission, and the current state determine how much may execute. A delayed replacement calls on the resident fallback, so latency-tail targets describe expected service interruption under the fallback premises rather than physical failure by themselves.

Whether the body can follow a candidate is a separate question from whether the candidate avoids obstacles. The Jacobian maps a tool-speed limit into joint rates that grow without bound near a singularity, and damped least squares bounds the inverse step there only by letting the tool lag its target; the manipulator equation turns planned motion into torque, and reflected rotor inertia turns a velocity or acceleration step at a seam into an outsized torque request. A quintic bridge matches the seam through acceleration, and time parameterization finds the fastest timing a path allows; that fastest timing switches acceleration abruptly, and a jerk bound, which costs little time, is what makes it executable. Sampling-based search, trajectory optimization, and learned chunking differ in how they find such a candidate and how much admission work it creates, not in the obligations it must meet. Each construction yields a better proposal, never permission.

The running machine's `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str` lease stops a stalled proposal stream through a state-matched response, leaving an illustrative `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.lease_margin_str` before sensing and model uncertainty. The alternate longer-lease case teaches a different limit: replacement admission closes by `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_alt_admission_cutoff_str` to permit physical stop onset at `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_commit_str`. Both cases preserve the same obligation to reserve response travel and the entire stop. On the base, even the jerk-limited S-curve, the shortest stop the load tolerates, raises the drive-limit stopping budget to `{python} PlanningC2Stop.total_new_str`, beyond the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.d_clear_str` rack-end clearance, making the runtime speed decision unavoidable.

@Tbl-11-key-equations collects the equations that carry these decisions, what each bounds or decides, and where each is derived.

| Equation | What it bounds or decides | Derived in |
|:---|:---|:---|
| $\Delta\mathbf{q}_\lambda = \mathbf{J}^T(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{J}^T+\lambda^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\Delta\mathbf{x}$ | The inverse-kinematics step near a singularity, capped at $v/(2\lambda)$ at the price of tool error | @eq-plan-dls-ik |
| $L = t_{\text{age}} + \Delta_{\text{da}}$ | Replacement latency from capture to admission, which the renewal schedule must absorb | @eq-plan-replacement-latency |
| $\epsilon \le \epsilon_{\mathrm{mission}}/K$ | The per-handoff tail that a mission target implies, far beyond $P_{99}$ | @eq-plan-union-bound |
| $T_{\mathrm{record}} \ge T_{\mathrm{request}} + Q_{1-\epsilon}(L) + T_{\mathrm{reserve}} + T_{\mathrm{stop}}$ | The time a record must cover, stop included | @eq-plan-action-chunk-horizon |
| $\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{M}\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{C}\dot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{g} - \mathbf{J}^T\mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}}$ | The torque a planned motion demands, evaluated by inverse dynamics at admission | @eq-plan-rigidbody-dynamics |
| $\lvert\dot q_k\rvert \le v_{\max} - \tfrac{1}{2}a_{\max}T_s$ | A sampled velocity limit that still holds between samples | @eq-plan-contracted-velocity-limit |
| $\tau_{\mathrm{request}} = J_{\mathrm{eff}}\,\Delta\dot q/T_c$ | The torque a seam's velocity step asks of the reflected inertia | @eq-plan-seam-torque |
| $j(t) = 6a_3 + 24a_4t + 60a_5t^2$ | The jerk of a quintic bridge, whose extrema the checker evaluates in closed form | @eq-plan-quintic-jerk |
| $V_{\mathrm{bus}} \ge L\,dI_q/dt + RI_q + K_e\omega$ | Whether the drive has the voltage for the current slew a bridge demands | @eq-plan-inverter-headroom |
| $\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{a}(s)\ddot s + \mathbf{b}(s)\dot s^2 + \mathbf{c}(s)$ | The path accelerations the torque limits allow, and so the fastest timing of a path | @eq-plan-path-torque |
| $d_{\text{stop}} = v^2/2a_{\max} + v\,a_{\max}/2j_{\max}$ | The shortest stop within deceleration and jerk bounds, above the plateau speed $a_{\max}^2/j_{\max}$ | @eq-plan-c2-stopping-suffix |
| $d_{\text{stop}}(t_{\mathrm{commit}}) \le d_{\text{clear}}(t_{\mathrm{commit}})$ | Whether a trajectory may be admitted at all | @eq-plan-commitment-invariant |

: **Key equations of trajectory planning**: Each load-bearing equation of the chapter, the limit it bounds or the decision it settles, and the equation where it is derived. {#tbl-11-key-equations tbl-colwidths="[40,42,18]"}

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Timed motion and independent stopping"}

* **Prediction is not execution authority**: A long predicted path can support short, repeatedly checked prefixes. Renewal cadence determines request throughput; target evidence retains its own capture-based age.
* **Reserve a response from the current state**: The matched suffix belongs to its declared entry state. Earlier lease or evidence expiry needs a validated state-matched fallback, available sensing and drive energy, and enough clearance for response delay plus stopping.
* **Admission precedes physical commitment**: The alternate arm schedule closes admission by `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_alt_admission_cutoff_str` to begin its stop at `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_commit_str`. A late proposer cannot spend that response interval.
* **A collision-free path is not yet followable**: Near a singularity a tool-speed limit demands joint rates the arm cannot supply; damping bounds the inverse-kinematics step but leaves a tool error and can still exceed the joint limit. A time-optimal schedule demands torque steps the drive refuses. A quintic seam and a jerk bound remove the steps, but interior jerk, torque, and clearance still decide execution.
* **The stop's shape sets its distance**: A finite jerk bound makes every smooth stop longer than constant-deceleration braking. The S-curve pays the least, one half jerk ramp of cruise, and that cost still drives the base's remaining speed restriction.
* **Rejecting a candidate need not stop service**: The current record can continue while its own state, evidence, lease, and fallback remain valid. A rejected replacement renews none of them.
* **Admission and enforcement need separate budgets**: Whole-plan validation scans bounded candidate content; per-tick permission checks current state and local evidence. Their execution time, memory, and interference must be allocated separately.

:::

The trajectory record joins the decisions made throughout this chapter: when to request a replacement, which motion the body can follow, how to join it to the current state, and when to stop waiting. Its conditions remain live obligations during execution. The permission path must therefore compare the running motion with fresh state and the remaining stopping margin on every tick, even after the complete plan has passed admission.

## Historical Perspective and Further Reading {#sec-planning-history}

Motion planning became a computational problem when @lozanoperez1983spatial shrank the moving body to a point in configuration space, and in the same year @schwartz1983piano treated the piano movers' problem as exact algebraic search, whose cost grows steeply with every added joint. Sampling made high-dimensional arms tractable by giving up exactness for a probabilistic guarantee. Probabilistic roadmaps [@kavraki1996probabilistic] and rapidly-exploring random trees [@lavalle1998rapidly] find a route if one exists as sampling continues, and RRT* [@karaman2011sampling] made the route converge toward the optimum. All three answer where the arm may pass, which this chapter treats as the first half of the problem.

The second half, timing, has its own lineage. @bobrow1985time showed that the fastest traversal of a fixed path under torque limits is bang-bang in the phase plane, and TOPP-RA [@pham2018new] later made that computation linear in the number of path points. The fastest timing proved too abrupt for real drives. @flash1985coordination found that human reaching minimizes jerk, @kroger2010online computed jerk-limited motion from an arbitrary state within one control cycle, and Ruckig [@berscheid2021jerk] extended it to arbitrary target states, the kind of generator that produces this chapter's stop. Optimization arrived by a parallel route. Direct collocation [@hargraves1987direct] came from aerospace trajectory design, and receding-horizon control came from the process industries [@qin2003survey], whose slow plants left ample time for each solve. CHOMP [@ratliff2009chomp] brought gradient optimization to manipulators.

The commitment side is the youngest. @fraichard2004inevitable named inevitable collision states and argued that a planner must reason about the states from which no control avoids collision, the complement of the viability kernel that @aubin1991viability had studied in control theory. Learned proposers then changed who generates motion. Action chunking [@zhao2023learning] and diffusion policies [@chi2024diffusionpolicy] predict short sequences from images, and real-time chunking [@black2025realtime] conditions each chunk on the actions already committed. What this chapter adds is the record: whichever generator proposes, the admitted trajectory carries its seam state, its deadlines, and a stop that runs without the proposer.

For further reading, six works trace the lineage from classical planning to learned proposals.

- @qin2003survey surveys industrial model predictive control from its first process-plant installations to the commercial packages of its time, the setting in which the method matured on plants far slower than an arm.
- @fraichard2004inevitable defines inevitable collision states and states the conditions a motion-safety argument needs, the formal basis of the commitment deadline in @sec-planning-inevitable-collision-states.
- @biagiotti2008trajectory catalogs the trajectory profiles used in machines and robots, including the double-S profile that @sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix uses as the stop.
- @kroger2010online sets out online trajectory generation, computing a limit-respecting profile from whatever state the robot is in at each control cycle.
- @lynch2017modern develops configuration space, kinematics, dynamics, time scaling, and motion planning in one notation, and is the natural companion to @sec-appendix-control-kinematics.
- @chi2024diffusionpolicy describes diffusion policies, including receding-horizon execution of predicted action sequences, the proposer whose seams and stops this chapter checks.

## Problems {#sec-planning-problems}

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-problems
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ GIVENS FOR THE END-OF-CHAPTER PROBLEMS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-problems.
# │
# │ Goal:    Hold the givens the problems add to the chapter's cells and guard
# │          each problem's intended answer, which the text does not print.
# │ Show:    the machine's 20 Hz renewal; faster validation and inference;
# │          FER joint-2 acceleration and jerk limits; an accelerating incoming
# │          chunk and a 25 ms bridge; the logistics AMR's limits; a late
# │          arrival at 270 ms and a 20 ms compressed bridge.
# │ How:     Registry reads (WarehouseMobileManipulator, WarehouseAisle,
# │          AMR.LogisticsAMR, FramelessMotor.TQ_ILM70x18) plus the earlier
# │          cells; answers recomputed in the private solutions.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg, millisecond, second
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    check, fmt, fmt_frequency, fmt_latency, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration, fmt_length,
    fmt_torque_constant, fmt_inductance, fmt_voltage, fmt_int, MarkdownStr,
)

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle
AMR = Embodied.AMR.LogisticsAMR
MOTOR = Actuators.FramelessMotor.TQ_ILM70x18

class PlanningProblems:
    """Givens that the chapter's problems add beyond the worked examples."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    f_renew = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen; chunk renewal rate, registry
    t_validate_fast = 5 * millisecond  # category: illustrative; faster whole-plan validation (P2)
    t_infer_fast = 20 * millisecond  # category: illustrative; faster chunk inference (P2)
    qdd2 = RM.arm.joint_acceleration_limits[1]  # category: datasheet; FER joint 2, registry (franka2023robot)
    jerk2 = RM.arm.joint_jerk_limits[1]  # category: datasheet; FER joint 2, registry (franka2023robot)
    qdd_in = 2.0 * ureg.radian / second**2  # category: illustrative; incoming chunk's acceleration at the seam (P5)
    t_bridge_short = 25 * millisecond  # category: illustrative; bridge duration (P5)
    kt_motor = MOTOR.torque_constant  # category: datasheet; TQ-RoboDrive ILM 70x18, registry
    l_motor = MOTOR.terminal_inductance  # category: datasheet
    v_motor = MOTOR.rated_voltage  # category: datasheet
    n_gear = Actuators.PandaClassJoint.CSG_25_50_ILM70x18.gear_ratio  # category: datasheet
    v_amr = AMR.max_velocity  # category: illustrative; logistics AMR drive limit, registry
    a_amr = AMR.max_acceleration  # category: illustrative; used as its braking bound (P7)
    f_amr = AMR.control_frequency  # category: illustrative; registry
    t_arrival = 270 * millisecond  # category: illustrative; late candidate on the alternate schedule (P9)
    t_bridge_late = 20 * millisecond  # category: illustrative; compressed bridge (P9)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────
    # Intended answers, guarded here and recomputed in the private solutions.
    _K = round((PlanningMissionExposure.t_mission * f_renew).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    _t_test_h = (3 * _K / PlanningMissionExposure.eps_mission / f_renew).to(ureg.hour).magnitude
    _L = PlanningReplacementLedger.t_sum
    _renew = PlanningLeaseRule.t_renew
    _inflight = math.ceil((_L / _renew).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    _inflight_inf = math.ceil(((_L - PlanningReplacementLedger.t_infer + t_infer_fast) / _renew).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    _inflight_val = math.ceil(((_L - PlanningReplacementLedger.t_validate + t_validate_fast) / _renew).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    _s = PlanningTwoLinkArm.sig_bad
    _v = PlanningTwoLinkArm.v_tool.to(ureg.meter / second).magnitude
    _lam = math.sqrt(_s * _v / PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_max.magnitude - _s**2)
    _T = t_bridge_short.to(second).magnitude
    _dw = PlanningSeamInertia.delta_omega.to(ureg.radian / second).magnitude
    _A = np.array([[_T**3, _T**4, _T**5], [3 * _T**2, 4 * _T**3, 5 * _T**4], [6 * _T, 12 * _T**2, 20 * _T**3]])
    _c3, _c4, _c5 = np.linalg.solve(_A, np.array([_dw * _T / 2, _dw, qdd_in.magnitude]))
    _ts = np.linspace(0, _T, 20001)
    _a_pk = float(np.max(np.abs(6 * _c3 * _ts + 12 * _c4 * _ts**2 + 20 * _c5 * _ts**3)))
    _j_pk = max(abs(6 * _c3), abs(6 * _c3 + 24 * _c4 * _T + 60 * _c5 * _T**2))
    _v_fit = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(PlanningLeaseRule.d_arm_clear, PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_path, PlanningLeaseRule.a_arm_stop, PlanningLeaseRule.j_arm_stop)
    _j_amr = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_amr, a_amr)["peak_jerk"]
    _d_amr = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_amr, a_amr, _j_amr)
    _v_amr_fit = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(AISLE.d_clear, AISLE.tau_delay, a_amr, _j_amr, AISLE.delta_loc, AISLE.delta_margin)
    _t_done = t_arrival + PlanningReplacementLedger.t_validate

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(_K == 12000 and abs(_t_test_h - 500.0) < 1e-6, "Problem 1 handoffs or test duration")
    check((_inflight, _inflight_val, _inflight_inf) == (3, 3, 2), "Problem 2 requests in flight")
    check(abs(_lam - 0.1071) < 2e-3, "Problem 3 damping length")
    check(jerk2 <= 4 * qdd2 / (1 * millisecond) and jerk2 > 4 * qdd2 / RM.chunk_step, "Problem 4 jerk condition at the two periods")
    check(_a_pk > qdd2.magnitude and _j_pk * PlanningSeamInertia.j_reflected.magnitude < RM.arm.joint_torque_rate_limit.magnitude, "Problem 5 verdicts")
    check(_v_fit > PlanningTwoLinkArm.v_tool, "Problem 6: clearance no longer above the TCP limit")
    check(_v_amr_fit < v_amr and _d_amr > v_amr**2 / (2 * a_amr), "Problem 7 derate")
    check(_t_done > PlanningLeaseRule.t_alt_admission_cutoff, "Problem 9: validation no longer misses the cutoff")
    check(PlanningLeaseRule.t_alt_admission_cutoff > t_arrival > PlanningArmTimeline.t_blend, "Problem 9 arrival order")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    f_renew_str = fmt_frequency(f_renew)
    t_validate_fast_str = fmt_latency(t_validate_fast, unit=millisecond)
    t_infer_fast_str = fmt_latency(t_infer_fast, unit=millisecond)
    qdd2_str = fmt(qdd2.magnitude, precision=1, suffix=" rad/s²")
    jerk2_str = fmt(jerk2.magnitude, precision=0, commas=True, suffix=" rad/s³")
    qdd_in_str = fmt(qdd_in.magnitude, precision=0, suffix=" rad/s²")
    t_bridge_short_str = fmt_latency(t_bridge_short, unit=millisecond)
    kt_motor_str = fmt_torque_constant(kt_motor, precision=3)
    l_motor_str = fmt_inductance(l_motor, precision=2)
    v_motor_str = fmt_voltage(v_motor, precision=0)
    n_gear_str = fmt_int(n_gear)
    amr_name_str = MarkdownStr(AMR.name)
    v_amr_str = fmt_velocity(v_amr, precision=1)
    a_amr_str = fmt_acceleration(a_amr, precision=1)
    f_amr_str = fmt_frequency(f_amr)
    tau_delay_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.tau_delay.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    delta_loc_str = fmt_length(AISLE.delta_loc, unit=ureg.millimeter)
    delta_margin_str = fmt_length(AISLE.delta_margin, unit=ureg.millimeter)
    t_arrival_str = fmt_latency(t_arrival, unit=millisecond)
    t_bridge_late_str = fmt_latency(t_bridge_late, unit=millisecond)
```

These problems use the running machine's parameters from this chapter's worked examples, with values marked illustrative standing in for measurements as they do there. Each problem names the decision it requires. The tags give the kind of work, from computation through design to critique, and the learning objectives, counted in order, that each problem assesses.

1. **[Compute, LO1] Exposure at the machine's own cadence.** Repeat \ref{nbk-planning-handoff-exposure-wall} for this machine, which renews its chunk at `{python} PlanningProblems.f_renew_str`, over the same `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.t_mission_str` mission and `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.eps_mission_math`. Find the handoff count, the expected late handoffs against a $P_{99}$ budget, and the per-handoff design target of @eq-plan-union-bound. Using the zero-failure bound of @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-survival, estimate how many hours of loaded operation would be needed to demonstrate that target by test. Decide whether the target should be established by test or made harmless by design, and name the assumption of the calculation most likely to fail in service.

2. **[Compute, LO1] Requests in flight and evidence age.** With the `{python} PlanningReplacementLedger.t_sum_str` replacement latency and the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_renew_str` renewal period, find the smallest number of replacement requests that must be in flight to sustain the renewal cadence, assuming each stage has the capacity overlap requires. Repeat with whole-plan validation cut from `{python} PlanningReplacementLedger.t_validate_str` to `{python} PlanningProblems.t_validate_fast_str`, and separately with inference cut from `{python} PlanningReplacementLedger.t_infer_str` to `{python} PlanningProblems.t_infer_fast_str`. Then find the age of the oldest observation behind any executed setpoint just before the next admission, and just before a lease lapse, and the tool travel at the `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.v_tool_str` TCP limit that rests on that evidence. Decide which of the two speedups is worth pursuing, and why neither changes what an executed prefix may rely on.

3. **[Compute, LO2] Damping for the joint limit.** At the `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.q2_bad_str`° elbow of @fig-11-two-link-singularity, find the damping length $\lambda$ at which the damped weakest-direction command for a `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.v_tool_str` request (@eq-plan-dls-ik) just meets the `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_max_str` joint limit, and the fraction of the requested tool motion it then realizes. Apply the same $\lambda$ at the `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.q2_good_str`° elbow and compare the realized fraction with that of the chapter's `{python} PlanningDLSStep.lam_str`. Find also the tool speed the exact inverse allows at the straightened elbow within the joint limit. Decide between a fixed large damping, damping that grows only near the singularity, and slowing the tool.

4. **[Compute, LO3] The contracted limit at two sample periods.** The arm's shoulder joint has a `{python} PlanningProblems.qdd2_str` acceleration limit, a `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_max_str` velocity limit, and a `{python} PlanningProblems.jerk2_str` jerk limit. Using @eq-plan-contracted-velocity-limit, find the velocity reserve for a checker sampling at the `{python} PlanningOpeningMachine.f_track_str` loop and at the `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_period_str` setpoint period, each as a share of the velocity limit. For each period, decide whether the published jerk limit entitles the checker to the smaller reserve of a jerk-bounded interpolant.

5. **[Compute, LO3, LO4] A bridge into an accelerating chunk.** Repeat the quintic of \ref{nbk-planning-seam-acceleration-jump-reflected-inertia-torque}, keeping the `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.delta_omega_str` velocity gap, chunk A's zero acceleration, and the $\Delta\dot q\,T/2$ position residual, but let the incoming chunk accelerate at `{python} PlanningProblems.qdd_in_str` at its join and shorten the bridge to `{python} PlanningProblems.t_bridge_short_str`. Solve @eq-plan-quintic-spline-matrix for $a_3$, $a_4$, $a_5$, locate the jerk extrema of @eq-plan-quintic-jerk, and find the peak acceleration, the peak torque rate on the reflected inertia, and the drive's current slew and $L\,dI_q/dt$ from the motor's `{python} PlanningProblems.kt_motor_str` torque constant through the `{python} PlanningProblems.n_gear_str`:1 gear (ignore gear losses), `{python} PlanningProblems.l_motor_str` winding inductance, and `{python} PlanningProblems.v_motor_str` rating. Check each against the joint's `{python} PlanningProblems.qdd2_str` acceleration limit, the `{python} PlanningQuinticBridge.taud_max_str` torque-rate limit, and @eq-plan-inverter-headroom. Decide which limit binds, and propose a bridge duration that passes all three.

6. **[Compute, LO5] Half speed and the speed that fits.** Repeat \ref{nbk-planning-stall-runway} with the arm moving at half its TCP limit, keeping the deceleration and jerk bounds. Then find the highest speed whose lease path and S-curve stop fit the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.d_arm_clear_str` clearance. Decide whether the clearance, the joint limits of @fig-11-two-link-singularity, or neither sets the arm's `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.v_tool_str` TCP limit.

7. **[Design, LO5] A logistics AMR at the rack end.** The `{python} PlanningProblems.amr_name_str` in the registry has a `{python} PlanningProblems.v_amr_str` drive limit and a `{python} PlanningProblems.a_amr_str` acceleration limit and closes its control loop at `{python} PlanningProblems.f_amr_str`. Assume it brakes at that acceleration limit, takes its jerk bound from @eq-plan-c2-polynomial-stop at its drive limit, and inherits the aisle's `{python} PlanningProblems.tau_delay_str` pre-brake delay, `{python} PlanningProblems.delta_loc_str` localization term, and `{python} PlanningProblems.delta_margin_str` margin (all illustrative). Compute its constant-deceleration, S-curve, and polynomial stops from the drive limit and its complete budget against the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.d_clear_str` rack-end clear distance. Find the highest speed that fits with the jerk bound held fixed, and decide whether to derate the AMR, lengthen its perception horizon, or measure a jerk tolerance first, stating what each choice would require.

8. **[Design, LO7] Choosing a generator for the conveyor reach.** The reach around the conveyor guard must be renewed every `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_renew_str`, the chunk policy's inference takes `{python} PlanningReplacementLedger.t_infer_str` at P99, and admission allows `{python} PlanningReplacementLedger.t_validate_str` for whole-plan validation. Propose a pipeline from the generators of @sec-planning-paradigms: sampling-based search with time parameterization, optimization such as the projection of @eq-plan-kinodynamic-projection, learned chunks, and an online jerk-limited generator whose reported worst case is `{python} PlanningTimeParam.ruckig_worst_str` on a desktop processor. For each stage, state whether it runs on the proposal side or on the permission path, what it guarantees by construction, and which check of this chapter it leaves to admission. Decide what the MCU must run itself.

9. **[Design, LO4, LO6, LO8] A late candidate on the alternate schedule.** On the alternate schedule of @fig-11-seam-timeline-fallback, a candidate arrives at `{python} PlanningProblems.t_arrival_str`, after the `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_replace_min_str` preferred admission and before the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_alt_admission_cutoff_str` cutoff, and needs the full `{python} PlanningReplacementLedger.t_validate_str` validation. Decide whether the MCU can admit it, and find the latest arrival it could admit. For a candidate that does arrive in time, fill the trajectory record's lineage, timing, seam, and content fields (@sec-planning-trajectory-contract), marking which differ from the record it replaces, and check whether a bridge compressed to `{python} PlanningProblems.t_bridge_late_str` still passes the torque-rate limit of \ref{nbk-planning-seam-acceleration-jump-reflected-inertia-torque}.

10. **[Critique, LO6] Waiting for a nearly finished plan.** A teammate proposes that the MCU extend the alternate schedule's commitment whenever the host reports that inference is 90 percent complete. Using the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_margin_str` commitment margin and the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_wait_str` counterfactual of @sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix, find the clearance lost, and the longest delay the margin could absorb at the TCP limit before sensing and model reserves. Explain, with @eq-plan-commitment-invariant and the definition of an inevitable collision state, why a progress report cannot justify any extension, and state what the proposal would have to change instead.

11. **[Critique, LO3, LO7] A chattering but valid policy.** A diffusion-policy proposer's chunks all pass per-sample position and velocity limits, yet after an hour of conveyor picking the shoulder drive derates on temperature and the gearbox shows early wear. A colleague concludes that the checker is correct and the drive is undersized. Critique the conclusion. Name the checks of this chapter that would catch the cause, state whether each runs at admission, at activation, or on every tick, and state the evidence that would distinguish a thermal budget problem from a seam or chatter problem.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From admitted plans to per-tick permission"}
This chapter admits whole proposals. The MCU checks a complete trajectory and its matched stop before the admission cutoff and latches the stop in protected memory. Admission judges the plan against a reachable state envelope, and activation checks the current estimate against that envelope, yet while the plan runs the plant can lag its reference, an obstacle can appear, and an actuator can saturate. @Sec-enforcement checks each tick against live state, insets the stopping distance by the tracking error the controller can bound, and owns the fallback ladder whose stop rung plays this chapter's resident stop. That inset completes the spatial terms accounted for here and yields a candidate aisle speed. Operating permission still requires complete capture-to-admission timing, positive stopping reserve, and qualification of the response under the declared conditions.
:::
